speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to make a few remarks on this amendment at report stage. Studying the Immigration Act was one of the
priorities of the Government when it came to office. We H increased the levels of immigration because of our concern that Canada be as open as possible. The Bill had a great deal of debate in the House at second reading and the committee gave long and careful consideration to it and to many amendments. We were assisted in this by Government and Opposition Members in an attempt to improve the Bill by making changes which would benefit Canada and which would give as fair a hearing as possible to people who wish to immigrate to Canada. I was not able to participate in the debate at second reading nor in the committee hearings. I am, therefore, pleased to have this opportunity to put a few words on the record with respect to this very important legislative initiative of the Government.
It is fair to say that we want to give every opportunity to people who immigrate to our country. We understand the problems in trying to come to a new land. Through this legislation and other initiatives we have endeavoured to bring the Immigration Act up to date. This is just one further method of doing that. I know that there have been several report stage amendments and I appreciate that there will be further debate on them.
I would like to take this opportunity to indicate exactly where the country is headed in terms of immigration. We have increased immigration levels in an effort to open our country to people from other lands. My Party believes that immigration is a source of strength for the country. By bringing in people from diverse cultures, we strengthen the culture of Canada.
Yesterday I attended a luncheon put on by the Greek community in Orillia in an effort to raise funds for the Greek Roman Catholic church. I ate some things I do not normally eat. They agreed with me, or I agreed with them. It was a time of happiness as we mixed together and enjoyed sharing the Greek culture.
I am pleased to have had this brief opportunity to put some remarks on the record which I have wanted to make for some time. I appreciate the latitude the Chair has given me in discussing this matter.

Motion No. 3

that the amendment of the Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford), while useful, is minor. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will indicate that the Government will accept that because it is a technical amendment which, from what I can see in the preceding part of that section, simply rounds it out. I do not think there is any question of principle. It is just a matter of drafting.
Motion No. 3, which stands in the name of my colleague, the New Democratic critic for immigration, the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), is a more fundamental issue of principle. 1 hope that the Parliamentary Secretary and the Government will be prepared to accept that amendment as well and will not give Members of the House instructions to vote it down.
The amendment recognizes that the membership in the Immigration Appeal Board has increased because of the Supreme Court ruling that there be an in-person hearing on questions of determination of refugee status. I think everyone acknowledges that there are real problems in having inexperienced members of the Immigration Appeal board making decisions which affect the very complex issue of whether or not a person is a convention refugee under the UN convention and protocol relating to refugees. The definition of "convention refugee" is as follows:
Any person, who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion,
(a)	is outside the country of his nationality and is unable or, by reason of such
fear, is unwilling to avail himself of the protection of that country, or
(b)	not having a country of nationality, is outside the country of his former
habitual residence and is unable or, by reason of such fear, is unwilling to
return to that country;
I have had experience with constituents and with friends who have been seeking refugee status. It is a process which I think everyone agrees has taken far too long. It is also an extraordinarily contentious process. I recall the cases of a number of people who came to this country from Latin America during the time of oppressive dictatorships there who sought refugee status. It seemed that the Canadian officials in those particular countries only mixed with the economic and political elite, such as their good friend, General Stroessner in Paraguay, or their good friend, the dictator of Brazil, or their good friend, General Pinochet. It seemed as though that was the approach taken by the External Affairs officials on the scene who were giving Canada advice on whether it was safe for people who sought refugee status to go back to their country. They offered advice as to whether or not it was reasonable for a person claiming refugee status to have fear of going back.
There is a movie showing in the city right now about one of the children who disappeared from Argentina. The parents had been killed and the child was given to a middle-class family. The wife was told not to ask any questions about where the baby came from. In fact, the baby had come from people who had been illegally and cruelly seized in the middle of the night, taken away, tortured and killed. God knows that happened. That happened to large numbers of people in Argentina.
Immigration Act, 1976
Things are now changing in Latin America, but it is a fact of life that there are still certain countries in Latin America, including Chile, and some countries in Central America, where people quite properly fear for their lives because there is no reliable judicial process. There is a dictatorship or junta in charge. I regret to say the Americans often support corrupt dictatorships, as they did in Nicaragua and other countries. Nonetheless, however it occurs, when people come here they have a very legitimate concern about whether they can ever go back.
What is suggested in the Bill is that persons appointed for a short time to the Immigration Appeal Board would be able to make what are life or death determinations for refugees. It should be amended to ensure that applications under Section 70 and 71 are determined by experienced members of the Board, and not by people who are there for the short time in order to clean up the backlog.
We are quite in agreement with extra personnel being added, if not in the numbers proposed by the Government, to resolve the backlog in simpler and more straightforward areas such as sponsorship, but not when it comes to the question of refugee status. That is why I hope the Government is prepared to consider Amendment No. 3 very positively. I appeal to Members of the House from all Parties for their support. This is intended to be humanitarian, and I think it reflects the fact that the vast bulk of Canadians are prepared to reach out, as we did with the Ugandan Asians and th Vietnamese refugees, as well as others from Southeast Asia, to people who have become persecuted and have to seek refugee status.
I want to conclude by pointing out that I spent last week in Westminster learning how the Mother of Parliaments works. I was very impressed by the fact that on issues such as this, which are not fundamental to the survival of the Government, there was a good deal of independence demonstrated, not only by Government back-benchers but also by opposition backbenchers. Members are prepared to exercise independence on issues like this, and it frequently occurs that the Government cannot carry a particular clause or amendment. Our House has just begun today to work under new rules which are designed to encourage greater independence by Members. Therefore I urge Members to consider carefully this amendment which is designed to ensure that people who are subject to refugee determination get as good a hearing as possible from IAB members with enough experience to adequately make the determination. I hope the amendment passes.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to speak very briefly to Bill C-55 at report stage. As you know, the purpose of the Bill is to expand the Immigration Appeal Board. There is a tremendous backlog with respect to refugee claims in Canada at present. I understand the figure is in excess of 16,000 or 18,000.
Twenty thousand.

I am told by the Minister that it is near 20,000. There is no question that that particular concern has to be addressed in a very forceful fashion. The purpose of this Bill is to expand the Board in order to hear more cases and get through the backlog. The Bill presumes what the reform of the refugee status determination process will be.
We have yet to come up with a solution to the problem, and as I understand it the committee is presently considering a possible solution to the problem. The Supreme Court stated on April 4 that instead of reading transcripts of interviews the Immigration Appeal Board must hear claimants before
February 24, 1986

making a decision. The issue is how to deal with the backlog, and Bill C-55 purports to come up with a solution to dealing with it. It suggests that the Board be expanded and shall consist of not fewer than seven and not more than 50 members to be appointed by the Governor in Council.
As you know, we on this side of the House have always been concerned about Governor in Council appointments. The record of this particular Government with respect to patronage is unparalled, notwithstanding the many promises they made during the last election campaign.
You know that the moment the Conservative Party took over the reign of power they started immediately to appoint friends and relatives. I need not go through the list of patronage appointments that were made. This Government has a horrible record, notwithstanding the promises that were made during the last election campaign. I only say that in passing because that is not the main thrust of my submissions. I have a concern when a piece of legislation gives to the Governor in Council, that is the federal Cabinet, the authority to appoint individuals. I should point out that as with other pieces of legislation, the legislation that established the security intelligence service provided that the review board should be appointed by the Governor in Council-in other words, the Cabinet-in consultation with the Opposition. That was a Liberal piece of legislation passed in the last Parliament. The reason why those words were added "in consultation with the Opposition" was to ensure that those appointed to that particular body would be above suspicion, and that there would be no appearance at all of a conflict of interest and that these people are neutral.
I would hope in the future that legislation introduced by this Government will include the same words, "in consultation with the Opposition", so that we can be sure that an end is put to the patronage.
Having said that I want to speak to the motion before us moved by our friends to the left. I am speaking to Motion No. 3, which in part states:
Subject to subsection (4) members appointed for two year terms may hear and determine an appeal or application made under all sections except 70 and 71.
The Member for Ottawa Centre indicated that the NDP are moving this particular amendment because when refugee status issues are determined one should have the more experienced Members determining that particular issue.
The concern 1 have with that is that this particular amendment would create different classes of individuals sitting on the Immigration Appeal Board. The committee in its wisdom amended the legislation to provide that there are, indeed, different classes of Members on the Immigration Appeal Board.
The committee moved that not more than 18 members may be appointed for terms exceeding two years, and a member appointed for a term not exceeding two years is only eligible for reappointment for one term not exceeding two years. So you have two different kinds of Immigration Appeal Board Members. You can have between seven and 50, but not more

than 18 may be appointed for terms exceeding two years. Now, we do not know what the length of those terms would be. I suspect the reason this particular amendment was moved at committee was to ensure that once the backlog is worked through the system we will not be stuck with 50 people on the Immigration Appeal Board because we might not need them at that point in time. I suspect that is the reason this particular amendment was moved at committee, but I am not a member of that committee.
I would hope that the purpose of this amendment moved at committee was not to create two different classes of Immigration Appeal Board members, because we all expect that anyone appointed to the Immigration Appeal Board will be qualified, or will render him or herself an expert on the Act in order to adjudicate on matters under the Immigration Act.
I hope that the purpose behind that particular amendment was not to suggest that those who are appointed for more than two years-the full time Members-should know more than those appointed for less than two years. The net effect of this motion would be to do that, because we are going to have two different classes. You are suggesting that those who and are appointed for a term exceeding two years can address or determine all issues under the Immigration Act, so they are more qualified.Those that are there for less than two years are secondary Immigration Appeal Board Members and, therefore, cannot determine certain issues relating to the refugee status of a particular individual.
For those reasons I do not intend to support this particular amendment moved by the New Democratic Party. It is well meaning, as are most initiatives by the New Democratic Party. Their hearts are in the right place, it is just that they have not thought out the particulars or the ramifications of the particular action they are recommending. I commend the Member for having his heart in the right place, and for his concern about the freedom of those individuals who have come to Canada and have requested status. Mr. Speaker, in the spirit of parliamentary reform I would ask NDP members to refrain from heckling during my remarks.
Look who is talking.
We all see the light sooner or later, Mr. Cassidy. Some day you might even see the light.

Don't get carried away now.
In closing I might add a few general comments for the record on the issue of immigration. I represent a riding in Metropolitan Toronto that is very multicultural. One of the biggest issues facing my constituents is the whole immigration issue. I would say anywhere from 70 to 80 per cent of my constituents who come to my office are coming forward with concerns relating to immigration. In an effort to facilitate the immigration process and to reunite families we should open the doors to those who are seeking refuge in Canada, especially those being persecuted in foreign countries. We hope that good legislation is introduced. While we intend to support

legislation that has that goal, we will try to perfect the legislation when it is introduced.

Mr. Speaker, no matter how one defines the board members, their number or the period in which they will serve, it should be kept in mind that a serious problem has arisen in this country over the past year and a half with an incredible backlog of applicants. The Minister chuckles when I say that this problem started within the past year and a half, but the facts speak for themselves.
While it is true that part of the problem arose because of a judge's ruling, the Minister will have to agree that there is a backlog of 20,000 people. No matter how many people are on the board or how long their tenure, the intent of the legislation is to process an extra 100 a year.

One hundred a year. Furthermore, when one considers the numbers that are accumulating over a period of a year, this will not even take care of one-thirtieth of the new applicants. The Government is not addressing the problem when it simply rearranges the number of people on the board and their tenure of office. The Minister stated in western Canada some time ago that this Bill would, unfortunately, address a part of the problem that is affecting Canada today.
A small part.

The Hon. Member says a small part. It is a very miniscule part of the problem. The fact is that the problem is getting much worse.
The Minister knows that the real problem concerns applying the refugee status. I am familiar with these problems in my riding in relation to people who are claiming refugee status, and the backlog facing the Appeal Board. No matter how one looks at it, this Bill will not do anything to relieve the backlog of people who are awaiting some action on the part of the Government. They have not seen action and, as far as I am concerned, we will not see it as long as the present Government is in power.

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-55, be amended in Clause 5 by striking out line 11 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"opportunity to be heard and time to prepare the case".
He said: Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members know, until the recent Supreme Court decision, the consideration by the Immigration Appeal Board of refugee determination cases was only a matter considered on the basis of a written record. One reason there appeared to be bias is that the written record came from immigration or consular officers in the country of origin. These records were well prepared and put together in the appropriate bureaucratic manner.
Many of the refugee applicants, on the other hand, might have been ignorant of the law or had lawyers who did not understand the refugee determination process very well. Furthermore, they may have had a poor command of the English language and had no way of communicating their sense of fear and the experience they had undergone in their country. Let me give an example. I understand that the Immigration Appeal Board has accepted 13 refugees from Peru. However, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), was in Peru recently and spoke to an immigration officer there who said that there were no problems in his country and could not understand why refugee applications were being allowed here. While this may be hearsay, it does substantiate the kind of problems that exist.
The Minister must know from her days in opposition that people who suffered torture in Uruguay and Argentina were
February 24, 1986

unable to persuade the Immigration Appeal Board of their case because they did not appear before that board.
The Minister has had the opportunity to be heard before the board while the applicant has not. This amendment would allow both sides an opportunity to appear. Furthermore, it also suggests that, bearing in mind the resources available to applicants, they should not be sent to a hearing immediately without time to prepare their case.
One could argue that this is a theoretical problem rather than a practical problem given the lengthy backlogs in refugee determination cases, if what the Flon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner) said is correct. The delays are such that any applicant will have had time to prepare a case before appearing before the board. However, we believe that this protection should be contained in the legislation in the event there is a short circuit process by which applicants from certain countries are rushed before a board before they have had an opportunity to prepare their case.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) must be aware that there were approximately 15,000 outstanding refugee determination cases at the end of June, 1985. These involve refugees from countries where there is ample evidence for people to fear going back to their homelands. These countries include Guyana and Sri Lanka where there has been persecution of Tamils, including a massacre that took place in a remote village recently. Jamaica currently has no parliamentary opposition. We know the situation in Iran. El Salvador and the Dominican Republic are countries in Central America where death squads are known to exist and the concept of human rights as we understand it here is unknown to them. While cases from India may have to be considered individually, I know that my friends who are Sikhs believe they have ample reason for fear over the treatment of their fellow citizens, particularly when the Punjab was literally closed off to outside contacts for almost a year. I have already spoken of Chile. Refugee determination cases are being accepted in Peru. Do Hon. Members opposite really consider that there is no case for refugee status for someone who manages to flee Afghanistan, Poland, Bolivia or Uraguay? In almost all of these cases we are talking about these kinds of countries, and when it gets down to making the decisions on refugee determination the Immigration Appeal Board is almost forced to let those people in. In fact, I believe in the case of Poland and some of the East Bloc countries, it is now the policy of the Government that people seeking refugee status from those countries will not be sent back because it has been established that once a person applies for refugee status their status in their country of origin then becomes so tainted they cannot go back.
I raise these points because I really regret that the Government is not prepared to make necessary changes in the Bill now, pending the implementation of the Plaut report. I would like to say as well to the Hon. Minister-and she can perhaps join with me in lamenting the inconsistency of my colleagues
Immigration Act, 1976
to the right-that the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mr. Pepin) in committee was in fact in favour the amendment which has just been voted down by the Liberals in conjunction with the Conservatives. In other words, in committee the Liberals saw it our way and I guess they have now been persuaded by the eloquence of the Hon. Member for Dollard to change their position, or perhaps they were persuaded by the anathema which the Hon. Member for York South-Wes-ton (Mr. Nunziata) displays to any proposals which come from the New Democratic Party, since he is one-time Member who some years ago abandoned ship.
To return to the question before you suggest that I do so, Mr. Speaker, I recognize that the purpose here is not so much a matter of broad principle as perhaps the previous amendment, Motion No. 3. The purpose here is just simply to ensure against the possibility-unlikely for now-that people seeking refugee status would not have adequate time to prepare their case. I would hope that the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary will be prepared to accept this particular amendment.
I would also hope that given the very large numbers of refugee applicants who come from countries which are placid, peacefufl and so on, but from countries where all kinds of things are developing, that we not go on with this sham that people have to wait two or three years before they can get their determination heard. In the case where countries blow up, as the Philippines and Haiti have blown up, whether from the left or the right, we must recognize that from time to time it is impossible for people to go back home. When that is the case, let us deal with them on a broad basis rather than on a case-by-case basis.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, and my fellow Hon. Members, I move not to support the motion because the amendment as proposed is redundant and adds nothing to the text of the Bill. Any appeal to the Federal Court from an IAB decision would utilize the ground of lack of reasonable time to prepare if, indeed, none was given. It is one of the principles of fundamental justice that sufficient time be given to prepare one's case. For this reason, I find the amendment suggested by the Hon. Member redundant and I recommend that the House not support it.
Mr. Speaker, once again the heart of the New Democratic Party is in the right place but-
You can sit down now.

-if those Hon. Members gave the issue a bit of thought, they would conclude, as did the Parliamentary Secretaray, that the amendment is redundant. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), in support of Motion No. 4, talks about Haiti and Afghanistan and the issue of refugee status, but I would suggest he address himself to the motion before us. What is the motion? The motion purports to amend Clause 71 of the Bill, which reads as follows:

Immigration Act, 1976
Where the Board receives an application referred to in subsection 70(2), it shall hold a hearing to determine the application, after having notified the applicant and the Minister of the time and place of the hearing, and shall afford the applicant and the Minister a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
The reason for this particular clause is the Supreme Court decision. What the New Democratic Party wants to do is to add the words "and time to prepare the case". Those Hon. members want the legislation to say that a hearing should be held and that sufficient time to prepare the case must be given to the particular appellant. As was pointed out, that is redundant. I would go so far as to say all of the words after the word "application" on line 7 are redundant.
The purpose of Clause 71 is to make it mandatory that a hearing be held in order to comply with the Supreme Court decision. We need not specify in legislation that notice must be given of the hearing or that the individuals involved, the appellant and the Minister, should have sufficient opportunity to prepare. As the Parliamentary secretary pointed out, the principles of natural justice would demand that one be given an opportunity to prepare.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the principles of natural justice require, first, that an individual be given notice-that is adequate notice of a particular hearing-and that an individual be given the right to be heard before a tribunal that is about to make a decision with respect to a particular issue. As well, reasons for the decision must be rendered by a particular board. To give someone sufficient opportunity to prepare almost goes without saying. If we give a person the right to a hearing and the right to be heard at a particular hearing, we must give the appellant sufficient opportunity to prepare for his case. The amendment is redundant.
I understand what the New Democratic Party is driving at. It is concerned that perhaps the board will require an individual to state his or her case on the spot, that a hearing will be called within a matter of hours and the person will not be given an opportunity to be heard. I happen to have a little more faith in the system. I believe the principles of natural justice would be adhered, to. If they were not, the appellant would have the opportunity to bring an action to ensure that he or she did have sufficient opportunity to prepare his or her case.
Would Hon. Members permit me to put a question to the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker?
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Supply and Services) moved
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-87, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the legislation authorizing the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited has reached second reading stage. Hon. Members will know that the privatization committee, as authorized by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget, has been reviewing a number of Crown corporations with a view to determining which of them no longer fulfil their public policy purpose. This task force, and all those associated with it, have concluded that Canadian Arsenals Limited, a company which has been in existence for a long period of time, no longer fulfills its public policy purpose. For this reason bids were secured from a large number of Canadian companies with a view to finalizing a sale, which is now under agreement with SNC Corporation of Montreal.
We consider that SNC is an appropriate purchaser of Canadian Arsenals Limited. It is a large, substantial and internationally renowned company with some 4,000 employees, 500 of whom will be the purchasers of the company under the agreement. The great majority of those 500-in excess of 95 per cent-are Canadian. Under the legislation introduced it is a prerequisite that at least 75 per cent of the company's shareholders be Canadian. SNC has fulfilled its obligation in this regard very well.
Canadian Arsenals Limited
The purchase price is some $92.2 million, which the Government considers to be representative of the real worth of the company. It is an extremely fair price. Having regard to the $50 million book value of Canadian Arsenals Limited, we think the Government has performed its obligation well in securing a reasonable purchase price for this company. The final purchase price was only reached after a great deal of negotiation with some eight Canadian companies, a process which took place over a period of months. I am happy to report that all of the participants have indicated that they are satisfied that the procedures which we followed in the bidding process were fair and reasonable and that everyone had adequate opportunity to respond.
We wish to recognize that Canadian Arsenals Limited is the only supplier to the Government of Canada of large and medium-calibre ammunition. It is perhaps appropriate that SNC, which is at the present time one of the very few suppliers of small ammunition, is indeed the purchaser. It will now be in a position to manufacture a range of ammunition for all of the Government's requirements. It will be able to devote the necessary funds to research and development and to give to this particular undertaking the necessary expertise and management which is required to ensure that the company be competitive and able to enlarge its export activities. This was a facet of Canadian Arsenals Limited which was lacking. We see this as one of the great merits of the privatization of this particular company-indeed, of all companies which we are considering under our privatization scheme.
SNC was established in 1911. We know that it is a leading Canadian engineering, construction and manufacturing firm with activities throughout Canada. Its assets are in excess of $100 million, and its 1984 revenues exceeded $200 million. The inference we are able to draw from these statistics is that SNC has in place the financial capacity and the management expertise which will inevitably guarantee the performance of its undertaking to purchase Canadian Arsenals Limited. I must add that of the $92.2 million in cash being paid for the company $87.5 million is for the shares of Canadian Arsenals Limited and the remaining $4.7 million represents the assumption of an outstanding obligation of Canadian Arsenals Limited to the Government.
This Bill was first introduced in the House on December 4, 1985. Arrangements have been made with the present employees, who number approximately 800, for the portability and transfer of their pension plans. There will be no prejudice resulting to the employees in this regard. Only recently was Canadian Arsenals Limited able to secure a labour agreement for all of its employees. The purchaser has agreed to abide by the terms of that agreement until it is able to secure an independent and new agreement with the employees after the purchase. The point is that we are persuaded that the employees of Canadian Arsenals Limited are safe and that their positions are secure. The undertaking and indication of the company is that it will continue to employ the great majority if not all of the employees. As I have said, there are

February 24, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
plans indicated for expansion and development for the two plants which the company now has in Quebec.
1 think that the only outstanding difficulty is that management of both Canadian Arsenals Limited and SNC are, at the present time, very anxious to conclude the transaction, obviously for the benefit of the employees and for the company. 1 would ask Hon. Members to endorse the concept of this legislation and approve it in order to allow this to happen.
The legislation, of course, will provide that Canadian Arsenals Limited will no longer be an agency of the Crown and that this company will be absolutely independent. There are provisions in the agreement to ensure that the continuity of supply of ammunition is guaranteed to the Government on a first priority basis. There are safeguards there to ensure that the purchase price of ammunition to be purchased from time to time will be reasonable and there are certain tests and safeguards imposed in the agreement to allow the Government to satisfy itself that the purchase price for ammunition will be reasonable on a continuing basis and that the Government will be protected in that regard.
I would be prepared to suggest that this particular legislation has proceeded without hitch and without adverse comment. 1 can only conclude that Canadians are universally satisfied that this is a right and proper decision and is in the best interests of Canada and the employees. Without further word, I commend this legislation to Hon. Members of this honourable House.

The Minister indicated in his remarks that Canadian Arsenals Limited was one of those companies which, in his view, no longer fulfilled a public policy purpose. My hon. colleague, the Hon. That is his area of expertise as our Party's critic for national defence.

The first thing we should know is that, although the Minister has assured us that there has been an agreement with the employees and that the employees were seemingly satisfied with the way this whole sale will take place, this does not at all reflect the conversations I have had with the people from the Public Service Alliance of Canada. As a matter of fact, those people were particularly critical of the Government for not consulting them previously and for not having been given any information concerning the portability and transfer of their pension plan. They have very little information about how the SNC pension plan works. Apparently they have not been provided with enough information on that. As well, they have grave concerns over the crossover to this new company. Therefore, I want to be on record as stating that at the time this legislaiton appears before the legislative committee we would like to have before us representatives from the Public Service Alliance. We would like them to state their case and enlighten Hon. Members of the House so that we can be assured that jobs will be protected, that pension funds will be transferred and that the total package of benefits the employees enjoy at the present time will be fully transferred the way the Minister says they will be.
Perhaps I should deal with some of the history of Canadian Arsenals Limited. As we know, Canadian Arsenals Limited was established in 1945 and it manufactures small and medium ammunitions. It operates a plant in Ville Le Gardeur near Montreal. There are presently 750 employees there. There is another plant in St. Augustin near Quebec City employing some 50 employees. We are not talking about a very small company, we are talking about a company that is significant in terms of jobs and what it has to offer. Were it not for the fact that the sale of this company happened at the same time as the sale of de Havilland, I have the distinct feeling that we would have heard a lot more about the proposed disposal of Canadian Arsenals Limited.
In the mid-1960s, the Government of the day in its wisdom had determined that a small portion of the ammunitions produced at that time by Canadian Arsenals Limited did not fulfil a public mandate and it was transferred over to the private sector. However, it was still the view of the Government that the rest of the operations of the corporation indeed were significant in terms of fulfilling a public policy. That was

reflected in Government investments in Canadian Arsenals over recent years.
I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the Canadian Arsenals Limited summary of corporate plan. All Members of the House have been provided with this, and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you have read your copy thoroughly, as I know you always do. However, in the unlikely event that some Hon. Members may not have read the whole thing, I would like to bring some items to their attention.
According to this Government document, in 1976 the Minister of Supply and Services confirmed the corporation's mandate. Ten years ago, the importance of this corporation was determined by the Minister of the day. A reorganization was ordered and revised Letters Patent were issued in order to widen the industrial base to include related military products, and that is what is indicated by the Government's report.
Substantial Government investments have gone into this company, Mr. Speaker. Let me outline a few to you: $3.6 million worth of modernization and $3.7 million for the recovery of operating deficits, a total of $7.3 million to be spent between 1977 and 1982. I know the Parliamentary Secretary will say that not all of those funds were used. He is quite correct. Not all those funds were required to modernize Canadian Arsenals Limited. Of course, the magnitude of the funds offered by the Government was to ensure viability and a good profitable operation. We know there was a definite commitment.
Let me read a little further for your information, Mr. Speaker. In 1982, the corporation took title to the moveable and immoveable assets located at Ville Le Gardeur, Quebec, the replacement cost of which was set at $25 million. That was in 1982, Mr. Speaker. In 1984, the company completed the installation of a new cartridge case manufacturing facility at St.-Augustin located near Quebec City at a cost of $13 million. Again, these are taxpayers' dollars. Some were profits generated by Canadian Arsenals Limited rather than an injection of taxpayers' funds per se. Because this is a Crown corporation, one can always argue that all dollars are taxpayers' dollars. Since 1978 the profits have increased tremendously and now total some $25 million. The shareholders equity as of March 31, 1984, was $44 million compared to a deficit of $1.2 million in 1977.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you have grasped this by now, this indeed has turned out to be a very profitable Crown corporation.
I want to briefly draw a few more things to your attention, because I recognize that many other Members want to speak to this important issue of the proposed divestiture of Canadian Arsenals by the Government.
First, it is proposed that the company be sold to the SNC group, a well known engineering firm. None of the remarks I will be making today, nor those of most of my colleagues, will have anything to do with lack of confidence toward the new company. We know that SNC is a company with a world-wide

also want to know whether there were lobbying firms involved in this process. 1 hope that the Minister pays close attention to this particular point, as he always does, because this is very important. I think I should speak briefly about the profitability of Canadian Arsenals Limited. On December 2, 1985, the Minister of Supply and Services and his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced the policy of the proposed divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited. One of the first things I did at that time was to ask for a copy of the last annual report of Canadian Arsenals Limited in order to go through it with the assistance of other people to determine how viable this company was, whether it was in fact making money, and what the impact would be upon the group which proposed to purchase it. I will attempt to answer some of these questions right now, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure you really want to know about this.
First, the profits of Canadian Arsenals Limited have gone up considerably over recent years. I draw your attention to page 6 of the annual report, which I am sure you have had ample opportunity to read. Page 6 of the report talks about the profits and losses of that company in thousands of dollars. In 1978 the company made $8,129 million worth of sales. Unfortunately, it had a loss in that year of $1,157 million. As the years went on the picture changed tremendously. In 1979 the sales of Canadian Arsenals	were $14,159 million and there
was a profit of $181,000. In	1980 sales	were	$30	million	andthe profit was $2 million. In	1981 sales	were	$45	million	andthe profit was $3 million. In	1982 sales	were	$57	million	and
the profit was $5 million. You see, Mr. Speaker, it is starting to become quite profitable at this point. In 1983 there were $87 million worth of sales and nearly $7 million of profit. Obviously you recognize that if people sold their businesses for book value they would not be very good business people. Businesses are usually worth a lot more than book value. Even if the information the Minister gave us is correct, and we do not know that, did the report also say that the company is worth the amount they said it was worth? Yet Montreal's diversified engineering outfit, the SNC Group, has just received a tough-to-fulfill mandate to turn Canada into a major munitions exporter.

Canadian Arsenals Limited
proposing to divest ourselves of Canadian Arsenals because we want to become a world-wide exporter of armaments? Is that what we are trying to achieve? If it is, I have some concern.
I read in the newspaper the other day that there seems to be division within Cabinet on whether to permit the Thyssen company of West Germany to make arms in this country for export to countries which are in troubled circumstances at the present time. Are we privatizing another firm for the purpose of sending it in that direction? If so, then I am really worried about the policy initiatives which are being espoused in this venture.

The fact that there is no competition between the two firms is not an accident. nation, but not to make it a major exporter of armaments to other countries. So again, very briefly, those are some of the concerns I have as a Member of this House and as a critic for our Party. Mr. Speaker, 1 cannot help but agree with the previous speaker in suggesting that although this particular divestiture of a Crown corporation by the Government has not created a great deal of public interest, that had to do mostly with the timing of the announcement rather than the concern, because there is a great deal of concern about this whole idea of the divestiture of Crown corporations.
The history of Crown corporations in Canada-I suppose in the world-is very interesting because in every case it is based on the need for development in countries. It is very interesting to note that the first probable Crown corporation, if we could call it that in Canada, was the Board of Works, which eventually became the Department of Public Works, and is now part of the Government. Other pre-Confederation corporations were the Harbours Board and the Nova Scotia Railway Company, companies that were established for particular reasons.
Since Confederation we have gone through a whole series of developments which were based on putting Crown corporations in key positions, as far as the economy was concerned. I suppose the first one after Confederation of major import was the CNR. The last one was probably Petro-Canada. We have gone through that series of Crown corporations being used as key developers in the economy of the country.
We could probably divide the development of the country into a series of areas or of times when particular directions of development were needed or wanted. Consequently the Government used Crown corporations as instruments of public policy; used them to develop the economy of the country by putting those Crown corporations in place. The biggest and the most common area of Crown corporation development was in transportation, the CNR, the Nova Scotia Railway Company and a series of other companies which were given support and
February 24, 1986

contributed a considerable amount to the development of the country.
That purpose of developing the infrastructure of the country, and using Crown corporations to do so has been a long tradition as far as Canada is concerned. In fact in 1979 when a review was done of the assets of crown corporations it was found that 49 per cent of the provincial Government in Canada-almost half of the assets of the provincial Governments in Canada-were held in the form of Crown corporations. Even within the federal Government 33 per cent of the assets of the federal Government are held in Crown corporations.
If it is now the policy of the Government to try and get rid of the deficit by selling these assets, we all know that the first sign of bankruptcy, as far as business is concerned, is when they start putting their assets up for sale. There has to be some good reason for the divestiture of any Crown corporation. I would question, along with many people of Canada, whether the ideological reasons which are being expressed by this Government are good enough for the divestiture of Crown corporations.
If we were to divide the country into certain periods from the time of Confederation until now, relative to the development of Crown corporations, we would probably say that first period was the development of transportation. At that time we had the CNR, Trans-Canada Airlines and later Air Canada. Those were established for a particular purpose. If they had not been, the development of Canada would have been slowed down considerably. We can say that in that first period of time Crown corporations were used well for the development of Canada.
I am not convinced the reasons that are being given now for the divestiture of some of the Crown corporations are based on any policy which has been well thought out, having to do with the development of Canada and the continued prosperity of Canada. If the ideology of the Party is being used as the basis for divestiture it is not good enough. The effect on the economy of Canada must be the basic concern as far as these divestitures are concerned.
The war propagated a large number of Crown corporations. Some 30 Crown corporations were developed during the war, again for very good reasons. Most of those Crown corporations were disbanded after the war. They were used to expedite the war effort and, except for a few like the Eldorada Mining Corporation, Palimar, which became Polysar I think later, and even the one we were talking about today, Canadian Arsenals, which are offshoots of the Crown corporations that were put in place during the war, they did the job at that time and then were disbanded. What we have in Canadian Arsenals is somewhat of a hold-over from that particular time.
The next period of time from the war-Yes, Mr. Speaker, I could come back at three o'clock.

THE LATE HONOURABLE T. C. DOUGLAS TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
"I am an ordinary guy who has done the best he can to promote the cause in which you and I believe". So said Tommy Douglas a short time ago.
This morning, at 10:45, Tommy Douglas died. He was a great man, one of those truly rare individuals who actually changed the course of history. He was a man whose life and work made Canada a better nation for us all.
Tommy Douglas was a Privy Councillor, a member of the Order of Canada and a Member of this House for 26 years; from 1935 to 1944 and from 1961 to 1979. In between he was Premier of Saskatchewan for 17 years.
As Premier of that province he and his Government broke new ground in almost every domain of social and economic activity. It was his Government that introduced the first Bill of Rights in Canada. It was his Government that brought electrification throughout rural Saskatchewan. This is something which he always proudly remembered and a fact that many people in Saskatchewan have recalled with a great deal of affection and appreciation. It was his Government that brought in the first piece of legislation that gave unrestrictive collective bargaining rights to people who work in the public sector in Canada. It was his Government that brought in the first truly modern labour legislation that treated working men and women as positive members of their community rather than simply people who had to be dealt with in some way.
Perhaps most important, in terms of its impact on our nation, it was his Government that brought in medicare to the Province of Saskatchewan, one part of our immense nation. It was an act that was soon picked up by other governments and became part of our national legislative heritage.
As a Member of the House of Commons, Tommy Douglas was a defender of civil liberties. Members who were with us at that time will recall that he voted against the War Measures Act which he saw, along with others at the time, as an unnecessary infringement on civil liberties. He fought relentlessly against the horrific build-up of nuclear weapons by the super powers on both sides of the global conflict.
He was a determined champion of Canadian autonomy in every field of human endeavour.

There will be other opportunities to comment on his impressive achievements as a legislator.
Today, I would like to stress his qualities as a politician, qualities which have had an enormous impact on so many of
us.

February 24, 1986

1 think first of his great capacity for combining passion and reason. Tommy demonstrated throughout his life that for our movement, these two must coexist. He knew it was not enough to make criticism of the society of the day. That can be easily done by anyone. "Our obligation", he said time and time again, "is to create alternatives which can command the support of the intellect". But in giving expression to this view, it is also totally appropriate to do so with passion. Tommy's whole life was an embodiment of the truth that reason and passion are far from contradictory, that in a political life seriously undertaken, they go hand in hand.
Over the years, Canadian men and women appreciated Tommy's superb sense of humour. More than any other politician of his generation, he brought to politics a sense of fun and the ability to laugh at himself. He was not sarcastic, because sarcasm always implies a desire to hurt. In fact, he had a very humorous outlook on life which attracted people instead of putting them off.

Most of all, when I think of Tommy, and my personal encounters with him, and I am sure this is true for many, many other Canadians, I think of his almost unlimited capacity for generating a sense of hope about the future. He never despaired no matter what the obstacle. That exuberant and hopeful spirit, based on the deep conviction that society should be organized for the benefit of all of the people and not for the privileged few, is what took him through all of the obstacles in his long and remarkable life. That is his legacy to us today.
Our deepest sympathies go to his wife, Irma, his daughters, Shirley and Joan, and to his grandchildren. Canadians all across our land join them in their loss of a truly great man.

Mr. Speaker, no one could have put it better than the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) who knew Tommy Douglas so well and who carries on the leadership of his Party. Many of us in the House of Commons had the honour of knowing Tommy Douglas well. I guess the younger Members of the House of Commons particularly considered him to be a historic Canadian figure going authentically to the grassroots of our country, particularly the prairies and western Canada.
As one of the signatories to the Regina Manifesto, he was the first head of a Social Democratic Government in North America and, as the Hon. Member for Oshawa has reminded us, he introduced medicare into this continent. He was a living legend to the people of Saskatchewan. At one stage in his parliamentary career, he represented British Columbia with great distinction as a leader of a national Party in that province. As I look at Stanley Knowles, I am reminded that both he and Tommy Douglas studied together at Brandon College for the ministry and his great Christian commitment
The Late Tommy Douglas
to the public good and public order followed him throughout his political career.
I had the privilege of attending the founding convention of the New Democratic Party as an observer in 1961 when Mr. Douglas and Senator Argue fought it out. I remember the great speech he made then. I felt he incarnated that unique tradition in Canadian political life beginning with J. S. Woodsworth, Mr. Coldwell, Tommy Douglas, and after him the late David Lewis, and now our friend from Oshawa. It has been a great tradition. I never heard a better orator in the House of Commons or on the hustings. There is something in Saskatchewan in those church basement rallies which brings out the best in the human temperament and in the skills of speech and timing.
He was a superb speaker. He was formidable in parliamentary debate and out on the hustings but he was never mean-spirited.

He was never, ever mean-spirited. I never heard Tommy Douglas take a cheap shot at anyone. However, he had an absolutely contagious sense of humour. I was sitting close to the late Secretary of State, the Hon. Judy LaMarsh, when he looked over and advised her to be a little more silent than was her habit. He said to her: "The Hon. Minister only opens her mouth to change feet".
Jimmy Gardiner once walked into a debate against Tommy Douglas in Saskatchewan. He said to Tommy: "What do you know about farming? You've never been a farmer". Mr. Douglas said: "I never laid an egg either, but I know more about making an omelette than either a hen or the hon. gentleman". It was his sense of humour and dignity, the self-sacrifice with which he clothed his life, and his public purpose, that made him a remarkable Canadian-indeed, a great Canadian.

The New Democratic Party has lost one of its founding members, one of the main founders of its movement.

On behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada I wish to join with the Leader of the New Democratic Party in saying to Mrs. Douglas the children and family how much his life has been valued by Canadians from one end of our country to the other.
I am reminded of the words of Longfellow:
Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives sublime.
And, departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sands of time.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has lost the voice and the vision of one of our great humanitarians and one of our truly outstanding parliamentari-
February 24, 1986

The Late Tommy Douglas
ans in the passing of the Hon. Thomas Clement "Tommy" Douglas, who died this morning in Ottawa. 1 knew of his reputation and his legend and, like many others here, was privileged to know the man himself. I knew of his personal qualities, his devotion to his church and to Canada and his love of his wife, his daughters and grandchildren.
Tommy Douglas was an outstanding Canadian beloved by all Members despite political differences. Perhaps the old Saskatchewan proverb said it best of all: "Tommy Douglas doesn't have to kiss babies, babies kiss him".
As the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition was speaking, I could not help but remember something which I heard him say once at a political rally. It was an example of the kind of humour he exhibited so well. He told of meeting an elderly farmer in Saskatchewan and in searching for a compliment he said: "Well, I suppose there have been worse Premiers than me". In the absence of any response at all, and thinking the farmer was hard of hearing, he elevated the decibel level and said: "1 suppose there have been worse Premiers than me". The farmer said: "I heard you the first time, I was just trying to remember".
I remember, as well, his comment about one of my predecessors in regard to a great debate that was going on concerning nuclear weapons: He said: "My right hon. friend is, of course, consistent. On Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays he's in favour of nuclear weapons. On Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays he's against; and on Sundays he's a Baptist like me".
Mr. Speaker, there was also an important dimension to Tommy Douglas which attracted Robert Cliche to his side. I remember well seeing both Douglas and Cliche in Quebec during those difficult years, difficult not only for his political party but also for mine, and that was in 1963, 1965 and 1968.
I saw the courage and dignity with which they tried to establish their political party on Quebec soil. Subsquently, Mr. Cliche spoke to me at length about his relationship with Mr. Douglas, his affection for Quebec, his respect for the French fact, his desire to set up a truly national political movement, and the courage he showed in the many positions he took in a spirit of understanding and solidarity.

I recall, Mr. Speaker, the privilege that I had in November, 1984 when I was able to call Tommy Douglas to tell him that I had the pleasure of recommending his appointment to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada. 1 was greatly touched by the generosity of his acceptance and of course his wit and his kindness. His appointment was in recognition of his devotion to parliamentary service both in Saskatchewan as premier and as a very distinguished leader and member of the New Democratic Party here in the House of Commons.
His passing is not only a loss to all Canadians but 1 think a gentle reminder that no honour was greater to Tommy Douglas than the respect of his peers and the affection of common people. On behalf of all Canadians, I express our bereavement for the passing of Tommy and 1 call upon this House to rise for a moment of silence.

I think of the air ambulance service and the Farm Security Act. Even though financial institutions took him to the Supreme Court, no longer could they take a farmer's land, home, barn and cattle. I think of the seed and feed grain debts which he took off the backs of grain producers and municipalities, and of hospitalization, medicare, and the Swift Current health region. Then there was automobile insurance, about which he once said that in a civilized society he thought that anyone who would make a profit from the misfortune of others was basically immoral. He brought in collective bargaining and political rights for public servants and Crown corporation employees in 1945-46, and in this he was ahead of his time by many, many years.

Speaking personally, when I was a green and frightened candidate for election the first time, attending my very First political meeting on a public platform in Leader, Saskatchewan, in May of 1956, Mr. Douglas was the guest speaker. The hall and street outside were full, and a public address system had to be put up outside. Earlier in the day his executive assistant had phoned me and said that Mr. Douglas would like to see me in his room in the hotel. 1 was even more nervous, fearing that I had done or said something wrong.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-ORAL QUESTION PERIOD STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Before proceeding to Oral Question Period, which will occur in two or three minutes, I think I should make a statement which was asked of me by the Hon. Member for
Oral Question Period
Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). Eleven years have elapsed since Mr. Speaker Jerome made the last such statement, and at that time the House was not televised. Television has had a marked impact on parliamentary behaviour, on the public's perception of parliamentarians, and on our practices.
The traditional guidelines regarding questions, written and oral, are to be found in Citations 356 to 371 of Beachesne's Fifth Edition. They are also summarized on pages 25-26 of the Precis of Procedure recently prepared by the Table Research Branch and distributed to all Members. While some of them remain valid, others have fallen into disuse as a result of the development of our practices. The House is the master of its own procedure and the Chair cannot enforce guidelines unless they conform to the will of the House.
For Question Period to function well-and for it to be seen to be meaningful-it must have some form. There must be some rules. As Members can imagine, several representations have been made to the Chair as to what those rules should be.
At one extreme is the view that the "old" rules should be brought back in their entirety, even those that have not been enforced for many years. At the other extreme is the view that the Chair should be concerned only with length and language, that in all other respects Members should be allowed to use the time as they see fit and that the public would judge appropriately.
A few even carried this argument to its logical conclusion, that Members should be allowed to use the time to make statements, if they wished, instead of questions, and to use whatever language they wanted, whether unparliamentary or not. If their voters didn't like it, they would act, went this argument.
In my view it would be practically impossible to go completely backwards to the rules which, for example, made it out of order to question a Minister about matters reported in the media, out of order to ask Ministers about statements made outside the House, out of order to ask certain kinds of questions regarding Government policy, nor would it make sense to do so, no matter what certain columnists might think.
On the other hand, while length and language are very real concerns they cannot be all that concerns the Chair. Question Period belongs to the whole House and, today, to a larger audience. While there may be political consequences, surely the House must be collectively concerned for the image and reputation and perceived relevancy of Parliament itself. If Question Period were to depart even more from its origins, to become only free-time partisan political theatre, surely that is not in our collective interests.
It seems to me, therefore, that the appropriate rules for Question Period should recognize the following principles:
One, the time is scarce and should, therefore, be used as profitably as possible by as many as possible.
February 24, 1986

Oral Question Period
Two, the public in large numbers do watch, and the House, recognizing that Question Period is often an intense time, should be on its best possible behaviour.
Three, while there may be other purposes and ambitions involved in Question Period, its primary purpose must be the seeking of information from the Government and calling the Government to account for its actions.
Four, Members should be given the greatest possible freedom in the putting of questions that is consistent with the other principles, or our practices should seek, in the words of Mr. Speaker Jerome: "To reduce to an absolute minimum the negative disqualifications that may limit or restrict a Member's right" to ask questions.
Mr. Speaker Jerome, in his statement 11 years ago, put his view with regard to the first principle of brevity so well that I would merely quote it:
There can be no doubt that the greatest enemy of the Question Period is the Member who offends this most important principle. In putting the original question on any subject, a Member may require an explanatory remark, but there is no reason for such a preamble to exceed one carefully drawn sentence.
It is my proposal to ask all Hon. Members to pay close attention to this admonition and to bring them to order if they fail to do so. It bears repeating that the long preamble or long question takes an unfair share of the time, and invariably, in provoking the same kind of response, only compounds the difficulty.
I agree with these comments and would add that such comments obviously also apply to answers by Ministers. I would also endorse Mr. Speaker Jerome's view that supplementary questions should need no preambles; they should flow from the Minister's response and be put in precise and direct terms without any prior statement or argument. It is the Chair's view that it equally follows from the first principle, that time is scarce, that Members should seek to avoid merely repeating questions that have already been asked. I do not mean that other questions on the same subject should not be asked-as apparently I have been interpreted-just that subsequent questions should be other than ones already asked.
For similar reasons it has always been a fundamental rule of questioning Ministers that the subject matter of the question must fall within the collective responsibility of the Government or the individual responsibility of one of its Ministers. This is the only basis upon which Ministers can be expected to answer questions.
Beyond these few restrictions, there are a few other traditional restraints that flow from the principles above. Questions should relate to matters of some urgency and not be purely hypothetical. They should not seek a legal opinion or inquire as to what legal advice a Minister has received. They should not normally anticipate Orders of the Day. However, I hasten to add that there is a normal exemption to that with regard to the budget process which I fully intend to honour. Members should be very careful with regard to questions or matters that are sub judice. Ministers should be questioned only in relation to their current portfolios and not in relation to any previously held responsibilities or Party responsibilities.
Finally, I would remind all Hon. Members of the citations in Beauchesne and in our rule book regarding language and
decorum. It seems to the Chair and, judging by the mail I receive, it also seems to many of our constituents that our language and decorum do not match those quite sensible citations and that we are not projecting the image of honourable men and women that is expected of us. Heckling and political quips are part of our tradition; barracking and personal insults must not be.
I intend to be as tough as I can in cutting off Members or Ministers in this regard, but there is little the Chair can do with regard to barracking from the benches on both sides except to appeal to all Members to realize that such behaviour reflects very badly on Parliament itself, and to ask again that we remember where we are. However, it is possible that excessive noise may blur the vision of the Chair and make it difficult to see Members rising.
As always, I seek the co-operation of the House in all these matters.
