subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mclnnes that Bill C-87, an Act to authorize the divestitute of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) had the floor. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the lunch break I was attempting to put before the House the concern that we in this Party and many of the people of Canada have with the decision that is being made by the Government to divest itself of many of the Crown corporations which have been established over the years, but particularly of Canadian Arsenals Limited. This is a firm which manufactures armaments. As I stated earlier, many of these corporations were set up by the Government over the years because the private sector was unwilling or unable to provide the necessary service which it was in the public interest of Canada to have provided. Many of these provincial and federal Crown corporations have been used, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. McDermid) stated, to pay for the social services we all depend on. We have here a corporation which is doing just that. In the last year this company made a profit of $11 million. Taking a business approach, is it better to keep a company which produces a profit of $11 million to be used for those social services, or to sell that company for $90 million and eliminate the profit? That is a concern all of us should have.
Given an understanding of how we can best contribute to the peace of the world, do we want to increase the number of corporations in Canada that make armaments and leave that sector of the economy outside the control of the Government?
This is the moral problem involved in the selling of this particular corporation. We consider ourselves to be peacemakers. We have a very well-established policy concerning the sale of arms. They cannot be sold to nations considered to be a threat to Canada, to countries with whom the UN Security Council has banned arms trading, or to regimes considered
10892

February 24, 1986
repugnant because of human rights abuses by security forces. South Africa and Chile are two such countries. However, lately we have had many examples of Canada moving into the world's arms race. Some headlines recently have said things like: "Canada supplies arms to Chile and turns a blind eye to their deployment". Or, "U.S. chases merchants of death", and the article specifically names Canadians arms going to parts of the world which are unacceptable to the Canadian Government. Another headline said: "Church groups alarmed at the increase of military exports". I am not suggesting that the group which is attempting to buy Canadian arsenals is going to disperse these arms illegally all over the world. However, we do know that armaments have ended up in the hands of the wrong people before and they will do so in the future. More and more arms with the stamp "Made in Canada" are appearing in Nicaragua, Chile and other places where they have no business being. That will happen more and more if we start selling arms for profit.
At present the Canadian Arsenals corporation exists because it supplies 90 per cent of its production to the Department of National Defence. That is the way it should be. However, do we want to increase the amount of arms produced in Canada for profit? Do we want to be part of the development of a war potential by our country?
I have a number of other concerns about this Bill. The Financial Administration Act requires that the Minister lay before this House any directives he gives to a Crown corporation. This Crown corporation had to prepare itself for sale, instructions had to be given for its sale, and the terms and conditions made known to those who may want to bid on it. However, none of that material has appeared in this House. I suggest that the Government has not fulfilled the requirements of that Act in this particular case.
There is another factor involved here as well, which I mentioned before, and that is that this corporation does make money. The Government, however, cannot use it. We have had our fourth divestiture of a Crown corporation. The Northern Transportation Company did not make money, de Havilland did not make money, and they used, in each case, the idea that there was something that was costing the taxpayer money, "therefore we are good fellows and we are going to sell it even if it did supply a private service or give us the kind of pride we thought we should have as far as Canada was concerned". We were proud of de Havilland as a national corporation owned by the people of Canada, but they sold it to a foreign corporation. In this case that particular situation could not be used as an excuse because this corporation did not lose money.
'
So what are we doing here-and this is what I would like to know and why I think the Minister should come before the committee to explain the policy of the Government-why is the Government they selling certain parts of the Crown corporation, or all of the Crown corporations? What is the basic policy behind this divestiture of Crown corporations? Are there certain areas or Crown corporations that are not going to
Canadian Arsenals Limited
be sold that are sacred to the Government? But that is a word that does not carry too much credibility with this Government. Will it proceed to sell them all off? This particular corporation, because it does not fulfil the requirements that have been established in the previous sales of Crown corporations, is probably a good testing ground. This may be the time when we should ask the Government and the Minister to come before a committee of this House to explain what their policy is on the divestiture of Crown corporations.
Regardless of what the Minister said in his original statement, it is a concern of ours that this particular sale does not have the real support of the union that represents the employees of Canadian Arsenals.
On December 4, 1985, The Ottawa Citizen suggested that the union was unhappy with the Canadian Arsenals sale. There was no consultation at all. This Government, which prides itself so much on consultation-although quite often it is just one-way consultation-did not really consult the employees' union and keep it informed as to how it felt about the sale of its company.
Before we go on to some other items we should also take a look at the really serious concerns that some people have about the Department of Supply and Services handling this sale for the federal Government, a Department whose basic responsibility is procurement. It is not a company that is well versed in sales; it is a company that is well versed in buying. We have been unable to receive from this Government any of the procedural background, although the Minister stated very categorically that it was done very democratically, everybody had the opportunity to bid, and that it went through four or five bids. I think that is probably correct.
There has been no opportunity for anybody in this House- as far as I know, unless it is for one of the members of the Government who is close to the Minister-to judge whether the whole process was above board. In fact, there have been some accusations against a senior official of DSS-although he have indicated by swearing an affidavit that he was not dealing with any aspect of the CAL sale-that this could be questioned as being a conflict of interest. We need an opportunity, and therefore we will be taking a look at these items in the committee when this Bill goes before committee.
As I mentioned before, the employees are not sure of their pension right now, after four or five months of the sale being almost completed, they do not feel secure about their pension plan.
We also have another concern, Mr. Speaker, that possibly some politics were involved in this. SNC was a large contributor to the Tory election fund in 1984. The Toronto Sun stated in December of 1985 that the SNC paid $1,000 into the campaign fund of one of the Ministers of the Government. Officers of the company paid additional funds into the central Tory campaign funds. La Presse also stated that SNC contributed in excess of $10,000 in 1984 to the Tory campaign. So these things also need to be investigated before we say yes and put the stamp on the sale of Canadian Arsenals.
February 24, 1986

Canadian Arsenals Limited
There is also the fact that SNC already owns almost the entire armaments industry outside of Canadian Arsenals. Val-cartier Industries, which at one time was part of Canadian Arsenals, together with Canadian Arsenals will end up being almost entirely a monopoly of armament production in Canada. It will be producing for profit.
There are a number of other areas which have to be investigated. If this is a method of getting rid of the deficit or selling off some of the assets so we can turn in that money to get rid of the deficit, is this a good business procedure? I think we should investigate whether, after five years or ten years, using the corporate plan of Canadian Arsenals, the net result to the Canadian Government will be better if it keeps this company or if it sells it. The Conservative Government, which prides itself on its great business acumen, should recognize that this kind of investigation should be part of the discussion which takes place before the actual sale of a corporation.
The previous speaker did mention the need to take a good look at the value of this corporation. As I say, it is already profitable. It is our understanding that its sale value is practically the same as its book value. Do we have any real idea whether the assets of the company that are being turned over to the purchaser are not worth much more than the $90 million which he is going to have to pay? all we have is the speech made in the House and the press release sent out by the Minister. There are no figures which would give us any indication that the approach being taken is acceptable and the amount offered is actually near the amount that could be received for this corporation. The agreements which are going between the two corporations are public papers. The Minister has not yet given any indication that he will make those papers available to us. It is the responsibility of Members on the committee to demand to see those papers before we approve this kind of divestiture of a Crown corporation.
I suggest that the sale of Canadian Arsenals is the first test case because de Havilland was sold under different circumstances. de Havilland was part of a larger corporation that had a mandate to privatize.
Canadian Arsenals was established for sound reasons. The Government believed it should have control over the production of armaments that are used by Canada and that might end up in countries that should not have them. I do not believe that the Government's reasons for selling this Crown corporation are adequate. When this Bill goes before the committee we will seek the information that will allow us and the people of Canada to determine whether the Government is selling this company for practical or for ideological reasons. This review will allow the people of Canada to watch how the privatization process will take place in the future and judge whether the Government of Canada is doing what is best for Canadians.
Canadian Arsenals is one of Canada's most successful Crown corporations. I find it difficult to understand why the Government would choose to sell a corporation that is third in profitability in the last five years. We must question whether
the Government is selling this corporation for ideological reasons-to show that the sale of Crown corporations is good for Canadians.
Some 90 per cent of the product produced by this company is purchased by the Government. Why is it divesting itself of its source of these products?
The corporation is required to file a corporate plan pursuant to the Financial Administration Act. According to its corporate plan, the corporation suggests that its sales are expected to double in the next few years, thereby doubling its profitability as well. When we are considering whether this is a good business deal, we must question whether $90 million is a good price for a company that may have a profit or $20 million next year.
We are also faced with the moral question of the production of munitions for profit. Many Canadians, including church groups, have stated their opposition to such a policy. This is another issue which must be taken into consideration when studying the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals by the Government of Canada.
Canadian Arsenals also suggests in its 1985-86 corporate plan that it would increase its production because it was motivated by the Canadianization of the products. However, according to an article arising from the sale of Canadian Arsenals, the Minister stated that the Government will purchase some of its munitions from NATO countries and that this corporation will be increasing its sales abroad to other NATO countries. We must question the Government's policy in this regard.
When the Government was in opposition it was active in passing Bill C-24 to amend the Financial Administration Act and make Crown corporations much more accountable to the Parliament of Canada. Now that it is in Government, it is ignoring that Act by selling this Crown corporation without giving Parliament the information to which it is entitled.
The Government sold de Havilland without requiring parliamentary approval. At least in this case the Government must bring before Parliament the sale of this and all other Crown corporations that were formed as a result of legislation. While I am not pleased with the manner in which this divestiture is proceeding through Parliament, at least the Government must bring its sale before the House, as it will with all Crown corporations formed by legislation, so that Canadians will have an opportunity to determine whether the divestiture will be good for the economy and the people of Canada.

February 24, 1986

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the sale of Canadian Arsenals to SNC. I had a couple of concerns when I heard about this sale. First, there is no way we in Canada should be left without a company that guarantees the production of ammunition for our use in Canada such as for our Armed Forces and, indeed, the sports world, which is becoming a very demanding market. The Government seems to have adopted a three-tier system in selling Crown corporations. First, if it can, it will sell these Crown corporations outright at whatever price. Second, the Government will chop a company in half so that it will be crippled in order to make the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) look good. That is the target. It is not whether or not the Company is sold for a useful purpose. Let us face the facts. Third, the Government will just simply close a company down, period.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
The Government could not care less what happens to the economy of the various regions or what happens to the individuals in those regions. Members of the
Canadian Arsenals Limited
Government have been making glorious remarks about increased employment statistics in various cities across Canada, but I have yet to hear the Government announce how many jobs were created in Chalk River. I asked that question the other day and no one answered me. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has no compunction about chopping Crown corporations. She will just whack them down. She does not care whom she hurts. She will just shut them down, get rid of the employees, but she will never call it a lay-off. "Lay-ofF' is a dirty word. The policy of the Government is to bribe them to leave, if it can, persuade them to leave, but never use that never use that nasty word "layoff'. What it is in fact is a simple decrease in jobs in a certain area.
Right now the Government is chopping away at the roots of Atomic Energy of Canada limited, another good Crown corporation. Canadian Arsenals Limited is a company which is quite a success story. Ninety per cent of its production right now is being used in Canada. One of its large customers, of course, is the Canadian Armed Forces. I am sure we all want to see an assured production of various types of munitions for all branches of our Canadian Armed Forces. That is a must guarantee with the sale of this plant.
I would also like to comment on foreign ownership. Because of the type of plant it is-there are only about two plants of any significance in Canada which produce ammunition-it is very important that ownership be retained by Canadians. I note in the guidelines that only 25 per cent of the value of Canadian Arsenals Limited is allowed to be sold to foreign owners. The preferable way would be to have it 100 per cent owned by Canadians. Another guideline seems to indicate that the company cannot be dissolved or liquidated without the approval of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes)-so he is still keeping his hand in-as a condition of the sale. But there must be assurances that a domestic source of ammunition will be maintained for the secure supply to our Armed Forces. I do not see that security clause in the Bill.
We have just heard some comments that it is bad to sell ammunition for profit. I do not know of any well organized businessman in this world who would go into business if he knew ahead of time that he would not make a cent. So I do not agree with that statement. What is wrong with selling ammunition to our other 15 NATO partners? There is nothing wrong with that. They are our allies. We are all involved in a common cause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: That's right. Speak to them.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
If we are going to sell this plant, I think it behooves the Government to ensure that support for this type of philosophy will be a condition of the sale. Many countries have munition plants which are owned by Governments. I visited one in Portugal which would be similar to this, although it is not as sophisticated as the type of plant we have here in Canada. Nevertheless, it makes munitions. So if we want to support our NATO allies with Canadian Arsenals Limited when it is sold to SNC, we should do it with lots of

Canadian Arsenals Limited
energy, knowing that there is nothing morally wrong with supporting one's allies in the goal of freedom for mankind. If we do not have our freedom, our moral arguments cannot even be expressed because we will not have the right to do so.
1 would like to know from the Minister of Supply and Services why he does not wish to table the Arthur Andersen Report which provides the details of this sale. In a letter to one of my colleagues, the Minister of Supply and Services informed him that the plant was worth anywhere between $80 million and $98 million. Surely, we have the right as Parliamentarians to see that report. If there is nothing wrong, as far as the Government is concerned, in selling the corporation, what has it got to hide? What is in the report? We know the company was sold for $92.2 million. The question then is, what is it worth? What about the $98 million figure? We also note as well-and this should be worth a lot of money to the Government when it sells a company to private industry-that there are about $200 million in back-log orders. Anyone would want to purchase a company with back orders like that. Why should they not be paying top dollar for it? The sales are projected to double in the next five years. The Hon. Member of Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) is starting to quote some figures. Just give us the Arthur Andersen Report. We will take a look at it and let the Hon. Member know what we think about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: You wouldn't understand it.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his compliment. That is typical of his gentlemanly-like conduct. The Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown always comes out with some very pleasant language in this House. He is an example of what the Speaker was talking about earlier today.
With regard to the conditions of purchase, SNC must ensure the portability of the employees' pension fund. This is a key part of the deal, in view of the fact that the Government of Canada did not see fit to talk to the union to find out what its views were on the matter, or even to discuss it with the employees at large.
SNC must complete the modernization of the Ville Le Gardeur plant and the investment may range between $40 million and $80 million. Whether or not the investment will qualify for 50 per cent subsidy under the Defence Industry Productivity Program has not yet been determined. I think it is important that we know what is in the report of Arthur Andersen. He was the Government's financial adviser. The Government said it would be open with the Canadian people and that it would hide nothing. Yet, here it is selling off Canadian assets and it does not want to tell the people what it is all about.
As a carry-on from Canadian Arsenals Limited, it has always been Canada's policy to try to provide ammunition and equipment which is inter-operable with that of other NATO countries. I certainly want to see this policy carried on when the Government sells Canadian Arsenals Limited to SNC.
As I mentioned before, Canadian Arsenals Limited will remain 75 per cent Canadian-owned. However, with an industry such as this, which has a considerable amount of security-in fact, it must have a certain amount of security built around it-I would think it would be in the best interests of Canadians to ensure that the plant continues to be 100 per cent owned by Canadians, as it has been since its inception in 1945.
I wish to say in conclusion that we cannot possibly let this moment go by without pressing the point home to the Canadian people that the Government is bound and raring to sell off Canadian assets left and right, if it can sell them at all. When it wants to sell off Canadian Arsenals Limited, which is a very profitable company, it means that it will certainly sell of anything else it can. However, I think the point must be made here that this is the same as having the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) secretly freeze the expenditures of all Government Departments about two weeks ago. Why? To make the Minister of Finance look good on Wednesday night. That is why. The Government has even cancelled the Canadian Armed Forces hockey tournaments because it wants to save a buck. The games are all down the drain.
I want to impress on Members of the House and on all Canadians that it does not matter whether it is a matter of DND school children, a matter of hockey tournaments or a matter of a Crown corporation such as Canadian Arsenals Limited, this Government is ready for sale. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that Canada is open for business, what he really should have said is that the Tory Government is putting Canada up for sale.

Mr. Speaker, I am totally taken aback by my hon. friend's comparison of DND school children with the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited. However, I leave him to his method of scare tactics. We are aware of how it is done in the Party opposite.

500 of its 4,000 workers will own the company. In any case, it will not be a foreign-owned company.
Members of the Opposition opposed the sale of de Havil-land. They put up a big scream. They said that it would be foreign-owned and sold to a foreign company. subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a short comment and then I would like to ask a question of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Renfew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins). First, 1 would like to congratulate him on his eloquent speech. I know that the Parliamentary Secretary would have wanted to do the same but he must have forgotten inadvertently.
I would like to ask my colleague a question since he is knowledgeable about military issues. In view of the fact that in 1984, Canadian Arsenals Limited made a profit of $8.5 million out of total sales of $97 million and that in 1985 it made a profit of $11,298 million out of total sales of $103.7 million, and in view of the fact that the rate of return on equity was in the order of 19 per cent last year and 21.4 per cent this year, is it the view of my hon. friend that we should not proceed with any part of this Bill until the Andersen document has been tabled in the House for the benefit of all Members of Parliament? Given these two things, and I have just illustrated for Hon. Members the ratio between net income and sales, and knowing that the Government wants to sell the company for less than the appraised value which it claims was made by Mr. Andersen and which it refused to show us, is it the Hon. Member's view that we should proceed with this Bill only after we have viewed the document?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is the message I was trying to deliver. What is the Government hiding? Why does it not tell us what it is up to? When we start asking for information on sales it tries to accuse us of being against everything. Perhaps we should dig up some of the speeches Members opposite delivered when they were sitting on this side of the House. They would probably recognize their own words.
I wish to straighten out one thing while I am on my feet. The Parliamentary Secretary commented about my comment on 25 per cent foreign ownership. If I have to, I will draw him a picture. I said that the requirements are that the company remain 75 per cent Canadian-owned. I did not say that it was only 75 per cent Canadian-owned, and I am sure the Hon. Member would not want to change my remarks.
With regard to what the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) just said, I do not see any problem with the Government tabling all the information with regard
Canadian Arsenals Limited
to this sale. If the Government is going to sell something and everything is on the up and up, what is wrong with that? There is nothing wrong with that. The record of dealings with the employees and everything should be put on the table. The Government should not create all these suspicions and then indicate that, just because the Opposition is talking about not getting information, it seems to be against everything. All we are asking for is what we deserve to have and is our right to have as Members of the House of Commons representing our share of the public of Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you know, during the last election campaign, members of Conservative Party made a great many promises to the people of Canada. My colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), has documented those promises in a paper entitled The Tory Collection, 338 Commitments in the 1984 Election.
In that election campaign, members of the Conservative Party promised to give high priority to parliamentary review. That was just one of the promises of the 338 promises that were made. During that election campaign, in their thirst for power, they promised to open up the Government of Canada in order to ensure that Canadians had full and complete information with respect to the governing of this nation, subject to the rare exception when highly sensitive material should be kept confidential. Other than that, they said that Parliament and through Parliament the people of Canada should be privy to information concerning the running of this country.
What happened to that promise of an open and accessible Government, a Government that would level with the people of Canada and be honest with them? We know now, 17 long and lonely months later, that those promises were but pure and empty rhetoric.
With respect to the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited, there is the Arthur Andersen Report, a report that the Government is keeping secret. It has yet to give a reason for refusing to make public that particular report. We in the Opposition have no alternative but to question the Government as to why it wants to keep that particular report secret. One can only conclude that it has something to hide. If this deal is such a good deal for Canada and the people of Canada, why not put all the information on the table?
With the divestiture of this company, Canadian Arsenals Limited, we in Parliament at least have the opportunity to debate the matter. As you know, Mr. Speaker, when the Government decided to sell de Havilland, we were not even given the opportunity to debate the sale of that particular Crown corporation.
I only want to say in conclusion that I agree with my colleague who has just spoken about the views he has with respect to this particular piece of legislation. I would hope that before the debate on Bill C-87 is concluded the Government and the Minister will recognize that Canadians are entitled to, and indeed have a right to, full information. 1 cannot see the Government of Canada asking for the support of the Opposi-
February 24, 1986

Canadian Arsenals Limited
tion when it is not forthcoming with full information on this particular matter.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-87 continues the ideologically motivated plunge into divestiture of Crown corporations without considering the matters from the point of view of what I think ought to be a more pragmatic approach. It is always an unfortunate thing to observe ideology overcoming good sense, but this Government seems totally committed to that point of view.
As the previous speaker indicated, at least the House is having an opportunity to debate this divestiture in contrast to the situation which occurred with de Havilland. I suppose that we should also recognize that at least in this case, there are assurances that the divested corporation will continue to be at least 75 per cent Canadian owned.
I think we should ask some serious questions, however, about the basic premise underlying the sale, but let us for a moment consider that we accept the premise. Let us for a moment accept that it is a moral and economic imperative to get rid of Crown corporations. Even if we were to accept that entirely questionable premise, there would still be some serious questions to be raised. Many of these questions have been examined in the media. Let us look at a couple of them.
First, there is the question why, in spite of the fact that dozens of companies expressed an interest in Canadian Arsenals Limited, only six succeeded in having their offers considered. We might also ask why the final bidders were forced to submit three revised bids between July and November 19, based, we hear, on the fact that the Department of Supply and Services kept changing its story. We also have to ask how we can pursue this sale under circumstances in which a senior official of DSS who is Directo General of Aerospace and Armaments left DSS on November 1 and went to work with CFN Consultants which, it turns out, was lobbying DSS on behalf of SNC which is purchasing Canadian Arsenals Limited. He may have signed an affidavit swearing that he would not be dealing with any aspect of the Canadian Arsenals Limited sale, but nevertheless, we are driven to considerable suspicion.
Perhaps, as was pointed out by the Financial Post, these peculiarities are explained by the fact that this is the first time DSS has had to travel the road of a privatizer. However, we also have to worry just a little bit about the fact that given this rather selective process of accepting bids, we note that SNC was a significant contributor to the campaign of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). We would also have to raise questions about the fact that SNC was a $10,000 contributor to the recent Tory election campaign. We must raise the question that ties in quite well with the expressions of concern on the part of those who failed to have their bids entertained as to whether this was a completely objective process.
We must also worry to some degree about the fact that SNC will now control both Canadian Arsenals Limited and Les Industries Cartier Limitee. It will have a virtual monopoly
on arms manufacturing in Canada. We must also take note of the fact that recently crates of IVI ammunition were found in the camps of Sandinista Contras in Nicaragua in 1982. This raises serious questions about the extent to which we will be able to control exports. I think we should ask other questions as well.
Canadian Arsenals Limited has been a very successful and profitable Canadian corporation. As a most successful Crown corporation making a profit for Canadians, why should we be selling it? Ninety per cent of CAL's sales go to the Department of National Defence. If that is so, why should we be selling it? Sales are expected to double. It is the third most profitable company in Canada, and it will become even more profitable. Why then should we sell it?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: That is a good question.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Unless we want to create a climate in Canada where arms are sold for as much profit as possible, why should we sell it? It seems to me that there are more serious questions to be asked.
Not too long ago there was an article, I believe, in The Toronto Star that pointed out the consequences of what Eisenhower called some years ago the military industrial complex. If one looks at the United States, one finds that we have a situation in which tremendous profits are made at the expense of the taxpayer, with repeated controversies over cost overruns of a monopoly industry supplying arms to the U.S. military, which has a complete license to charge taxpayers whatever it may choose, of corruption gone uncontrolled and unstoppable in a situation where private enterprise has complete rein in supplying arms and munitions. It is a situation that causes moral bankruptcy.
It is a situation which in Canada need not exist. Yet we are told that under privatization Canadian Arsenals Limited will expand and will probably expand its product and engage in the merchanting of arms all over the world. We hear references to the sale of arms to Third World nations. I do not know whether that is the sort of thing that the Canadian taxpayer wants to see.
I think the Canadian taxpayer does not want to see its Armed Forces well armed with high quality armaments. I do not think Canadians want to see a situation which will change the circumstances of reasonable profits being earned by reasonable costs. I do not think the taxpayers see any necessity for Canada earning income by becoming a competing merchant on the world scene selling arms to nations which ought to have higher priorities for feeding their people instead of pursuing the path of war. 1 do not see the justification for this.
I want to ask Members opposite what their defence is for the sale of a profitable company, what their defence is for placing the sale of armaments and munitions in the hands of private industry, what their response is to the concern of Canadians that we not follow the path of our southern neighbors where armaments become the focus of the entire economic status of a

February 24, 1986
nation. 1 ask all Members to consider very carefully the implications of legislation which at the same time abandons the taxpayers' company and the potential for reasonable profit and reasonable sales of munitions versus a situation in which we will increase our status as merchandisers of death around the world.

Mr. Speaker, I think I should point out to the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) that he continually referred to selling the munitions industry in Canada to the private sector. I am sure the Member is well aware, and 1 would not want him inadvertently to give the wrong impression. In reality, all other munitions manufacturers in Canada are privately owned. Of the five major manufacturers, only the one, Canadian Arsenals Limited, is a Crown corporation.
The Member referred to the fact that we would be exporting munitions with this venture. If SNC expands Canadian Arsenals' base and creates jobs east of Montreal in an area about which we are very concerned and which his Party and the other Party beside him have made many points about in the last little while, I will not oppose that expansion and creation of jobs in the east Montreal area; I will applaud them.

Our Party says that there are too many other needs to be met in this country, too many jobs that could be created by fulfilling real needs than having us try to create jobs in any way, shape or form through the sale of munitions to anyone.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
speechtext:
That:
Whereas 1985 is the centenary of the Northwest Resistance, the most important event in the history of the Metis Nation and a milestone in the history of Canada; and
Whereas the leader of the Metis people, Louis David Riel, was executed for his role in that resistance; and
Whereas Louis David Riel negotiated Manitoba's entry into Confederation and was thrice elected to the House of Commons; and
Whereas the Metis people have continued to strive, since the death of Louis David Riel, for the recognition of their rights; and
Whereas the Constitution Act. 1982 recognized and affirmed the rights of the Metis people;
Be it resolved that this House
1.	acknowledge the significant contributions of the Metis people to the
development of the West and the creation of Canada;
2.	recognize Louis David Riel as the founder of Manitoba and a father of
Confederation;
3.	celebrate with the Metis their unique culture and heritage;
4.	support self-government and a land base for the Metis.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution was motivated by the fact that last year, 1985, marked the centenary of the so-called Northwest Resistance, or the Northwest Rebellion, considered to be the most important event in the history of the Metis
February 24, 1986

February 24, 1986
as the president, and this list of rights was sent to Ottawa. The House may be interested in what that list of rights contained. Here it is. An elected local legislature. Representation in the Canadian Parliament. Appropriation of public lands for roads and schools. The official languages to be French and English. Winnipeg to be connected with the nearest railway. A steamboat connecting Lake Superior and Red River within five years. The franchise to be granted to every man over 21. Confirmation of all existing privileges, customs and usages.
There was nothing very radical or revolutionary there, nothing that any of us in this House can object to, except, perhaps, the limited franchise to men over 21. However, that was still the unfortunate norm of the day and it is difficult to criticise except in retrospect. Nevertheless, as I said a moment ago, there was some opposition and resistance in the community. There followed arrests and one prisoner, Thomas Scott, was executed by firing squad. The new Canadian Encyclopedia, which has enjoyed such great success across the country, refers to this Red River rebellion as being a movement of national self-determination by the Metis of the Red River colony.
Well, if there was some resentment by a few people in the colony, there was also a controversy back here in eastern Canada. Despite the controversy over what Riel was doing, in 1870 the Manitoba Act was passed by the Parliament of Canada. It incorporated many of the rights which I quoted earlier from the Metis list of rights which had been drawn up by Louis Riel and his close advisers and approved by the convention he had called. Under the Manitoba Act of 1870 the Metis were to receive 1.4 million acres of land. Now, time does not allow me to describe the full and sad history which reveals how that land was either kept from these people or tricked away from them by one means or another, often with the banks being the major culprits. I should point out that after the passage of this Act, amnesty was granted to all who had participated in the uprising at the Red River community. Only Riel was exempted from that amnesty because it was alleged that he had played an important part in the death of Thomas Scott. So, for several years Riel remained a fugitive. However, during that period of time he was elected to the Parliament of Canada three times but was prevented on each occasion from taking his seat in this House. Finally, in 1875, Riel himself was given amnesty provided that he was prepared to leave the country, his home and his land, for a five-year banishment.
With his departure, Sir, the Metis people of the Red River began to disperse. They moved out of Manitoba, westward along the South Saskatchewan River, and there faced exactly the same problems they had faced back home. There were questions about their legal right to the land. There were those pesky surveyors once again with their preconceived ideas of how the land should be carved up and divided. So, in frustration, once more the people sent a delegation to see Riel who was now teaching school in Montana. He was asked to come back, and he did. In a meeting held in Prince Albert he urged all those in attendance, Metis, whites and Indians alike, to present their grievances to Ottawa. So you can see that already western alienation was beginning to take form. They were to
Metis Nation
present their grievances to Ottawa just as Members of Parliament from western Canada and other parts of the country present their regional grievances in one way or another to this House. Petitions were sent and, just as today, or at least before we adopted our new rules, there was no response to those petitions. So Riel discovered that the co-operation he had tried to build up among the different groups began to wane. However, there was one issue which, more than anything else, caused division, and that was the question of aboriginal rights. Does that not sound familiar? It is a question which still plagues us as we move closer to the 21st century. Riel once again resorted to a route that he was familiar with, that of the provisional Government which was proclaimed at Batoche on March 19, 1885. However, this time the situation was different. The Northwest Mounted Police were in place. It was easy to bring a militia and weapons into the area by means of the railway, and so the armed engagements of the Northwest Rebellion commenced.
The militia, under General Middleton, was sent in. There was some very, very fierce fighting and, in due course, the rebellion was quelled. Riel surrendered, was taken to Regina as a prisoner, tried by a six-man jury, and found guilty of treason. He was hanged in Regina on November 16, 1885. Sir, I believe that was a dark day for Canada. It was an event which now symbolizes injustice for the Metis people. They regard it as a cynical act, political in nature and carrying with it all of the ugly implications of racism. This despicable act is a constant reminder of the social, economic and political injustice done to our first citizens, the aboriginal people, the Metis people of the new West.
The need to somehow correct this historical injustice is, from time to time, discussed and considered by scholars, and even Members of this House. However, the idea of a pardon for Riel by the Canadian Government is now rejected by the Metis people and their leaders because a pardon, it is believed, would only serve to perpetuate the alleged guilt and make legitimate a political murder. Riel was the leader of a democratic revolution. It was the Metis who led Manitoba into Confederation and Louis Riel is the Metis father of Confederation. He rebelled against oppression, which I have described briefly but which was really much more serious than mere words can convey in a short time. He contributed to the cause of freedom and led the Metis struggle for freedom, a struggle which goes on even today.
In 1932, at a meeting in St. Albert in the Province of Alberta, the Metis Association of Alberta was formed and the minutes of that meeting are available to us. I would like to read just the opening paragraph from those minutes because they enunciate for us a basic Metis principle. It says:
The history of our country shows that we have given service and sacrificed much in the upbuilding of the west. We have suffered as a result, but we do not forget that we are a responsible race and are prepared to play our part in the upbuilding of this country, Canada.
Today the Metis people have won recognition in our new Constitution. They are demanding their rightful place in the
February 24, 1986

Metis Nation
Confederation of Canada. Those among them who are dispossessed and who are among the poorest of the poor are seeking a land base. Others, who live in an urban environment, want some say and some influence over the various institutions that impact and impinge on their lives. A recent policy paper from the new Ontario Government says, "They may wish to receive guaranteed participation in existing legislatures, school boards and other special purpose bodies".
The one greatest priority, Sir, and I end on this note, is their need for economic development, special programs which they manage and which can lead them out of the dreadful poverty cycle in which they find themselves. When the resolution talks about self-government or self-determination it is those kind of goals that are referred to, goals that are reasonable and obtainable. 1 ask this House to consider carefully and to give its consent to this resolution. It is submitted on behalf of the Metis people of Canada, and if we were to respond to it positively, I believe we would be acting in the spirit of our new Canadian Constitution, which recognizes that the Metis people are one of the three major aboriginal groups in our nation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, today is a very, very special day for me and my father in that I became a proud grandfather and he a great-grandfather for the first time.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
speechtext:
I am honoured to speak of my Metis heritage during this debate, only hoping that the words and the thoughts that I convey today will one day show my new granddaughter that she has a special heritage and a family history to be really proud of.
I would like to take this opportunity to express my views on the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). At this time I would like to point out that without question I know that the intentions of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior are above reproach. I think all Canadians can look to the Metis heritage with pride, recognizing in it a strength and vision which characterized the mixture of Indian blood lines with those of our early European settlers, and which continue even up to today. The motion presented to us this afternoon seems to consist of two very different issues; the recognition of Louis David Riel as a national figure, which is undoubtedly an important step in the right direction, and the issue of self-government and land claims by the Metis people of this country.
I would first like to mention that as a Metis brought up in Manitoba I am fully aware of the important contributions of the Metis people in the development of the western provinces. There can be no question of the importance of Louis Riel's support in giving direction and inspiration to the Metis people in their participation in the Canadian Confederation.
This motion seeks recognition, not only for the Metis of Canada but also for their recognized leader, Louis David Riel.
The question of whether Louis Riel should be recognized as a father of Confederation is interesting, and at the same time
seems a bit irrelevant. I would like to clarify that. In explaining my vision of Riel's commitment to Canada, I would like to speak briefly on the question of whether Riel should be recognized as a Father of Confederation. This is an interesting one. Certainly he should be recognized as a prime mover of Manitoba into Confederation, but what is a Father of Confederation? It appears that there is no official list of Fathers of Confederation, only a traditional list. Tradition in Canada has been to refer to the delegate at the three pre-Confederation conferences as Fathers of Confederation. TThese conferences were in Charlottetown and in Quebec in 1864 and in London in 1867, and comprised some 34 delegates. No official protocol list exists that describes the Fathers of Confederation. Many will point out that Joey Smallwood has frequently affectionately been referred to as the only living Father of Confederation. This appellation pays homage to his contribution of bringing Newfoundland into Confederation. Even this designation is based on usage rather than on legality. In fact, he is not a Father of Confederation. Extending the logic of pre-Confederation conferences, if Mr. Smallwood is a Father of Confederation, so too are all of the other signatories at the Ottawa conference in 1949, which led to the entry of Newfoundland into the Union. I am referring to Louis St. Laurent, Gordon Bradley and many others who were all signatories at this time.
You can see that there is no easy formula to determine who is a Father of Confederation. It could create a dangerous precedent to be selective as to who we assign that designate to. In effect, each province has its own history of pre and post Confederation development. Each is equally important to the Canada that we know today.
In clarifying my vision of Riel's commitment to Canada, I think Riel should be honoured as a truly great Canadian and should stand alone on his own merits. Riel not only contributed to the formation of this great nation, he went even further, he laid down his life for that very cause. I honestly believe that this legislation cannot change the course of history, and that Riel's role cannot be limited to that of a Father of Confederation. He represents more than just a political figure, he is a maker of history.
Consultations have taken place with Metis leaders prior to the introduction of this motion before the House, but I am of the understanding that no consultations took part with the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior. I have spoken to the leaders of the Metis movement just as recently as this morning and they informed me that they have not been consulted. Possibly he has met with them. He stated in his delivery that he had and, as I say, I do not question the integrity or the intentions of the Hon. Member. In my discussions with them, they stated that no consultation had taken place prior to the presentation of this motion to the House. In the past the Liberal Party paid only lip service to the plight of the Metis. It actually used us for political expedience, and only now is it examining the possibility of giving that national hero the medal that he deserved 100 years ago. History cannot be corrected 100 years later. Certain Parties have always tried to portray themselves as the great saviours of the Metis cause.

February 24, 1986
but what did they actually do for the Metis of the West? I will tell you what they did, they spoke of the poverty we lived in, prejudices we were subjected to, the lack of educational opportunities that they spoke of, but they did nothing about them. There were family upheavals and discrimination. 1 know what grave injustices were done, I lived them. 1 spoke to Angus Spence before he passed on so suddenly last year. He was a prime mover and shaker within the Metis organization in Manitoba. He told me of the discrimination that he lived with in his part of Manitoba, of the religious discrimination that existed even among the Metis that was brought upon them because of the discrimination within the Province of Manitoba. It seemed that the darker one's skin as a result of one's ancestral background, the more the discrimination. I have lived it.
Previous Governments had somehow hoped that the guilt that had been borne by all Canadians would simply disappear like a bad dream. But we remember, and we only wish that Riel will rest in peace and be honoured as a true patriot. We do not want this to carry on. We want Riel to take his rightful place as a Canadian. As Metis, we do not want a preferential spot; we want an equal spot like the place held by every other Canadian in this great Canadian mosaic.
Riel was three times elected to the House and represented the Provencher constituency during a very unstable political period. If we try to understand the forces on the political stage at that time, we realize that there is no doubt that the Metis people and Riel played a vital role in the founding of Manitoba. There is no doubt that Riel is a true national figure.
Let me speak briefly to the second element of this motion. As my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior knows, land claims are now under review by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). There is no doubt that their land was taken from them. The Hon. Member spoke of long river lots that were inhabited by my grandfather, Jean Baptiste St. Germain, Louis Zastre, the Monette and the St. Denis families along the Assiniboine and Red Rivers. Some of them managed to maintain their lands but much of it was taken.
When we go back to the history of La Prairie du Cheval Blanc we recall the names of Cuthbert Grant, Pascal Breland and up to the time of Angus Spence. We think of those who worked so fervently to improve the plight of the Metis.
There is no doubt that injustices were done at that time. But again, I go back to the original motion. I believe we are dealing with two important issues but one is clouded by the other if we do not deal with them separately. Riel is a true national hero. I do not understand the relationship between the two aspects of the Hon. Member's motion. Hopefully, all of the items raised by the Hon. Member will be resolved to the satisfaction of those who were so adversely affected.
Let me reiterate my position as a Metis. I am proud of my ancestry. I thank the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior for his wish for recognition of the national Metis hero, Louis
Metis Nation
David Riel. Riel cannot be resurrected from the dead and we can only try to learn by history's lessons. We must always remember that our duty is to seek to do justice within our own time.
I have spoken to members of the Metis organizations across the country. I want to consult with all Parties in the House in seeking to establish a true method of recognizing Louis David Riel for the great Canadian he was. I will be taking it upon myself to consult with the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) in the hope that we can establish a unanimous consensus as Canadians and politicians in bringing forward a resolution that would be acceptable to all and would truly reflect what Riel was and what he contributed.
I would like to make my last words in the debate those of Louis Riel, who was never able to offer them in the House. He said:
[ Translation]
"One's country is the most important thing on this earth, and it is hallowed by the traditions of one's ancestors".

Let us reflect on this man's heroic stance in our nation's history and not resurrect our past mistakes but go on to build a better, stronger and proud Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HISTORIC EVENTS SUGGESTED REAFFIRMATION OF METIS RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to debate the resolution that has been submitted by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). This is not the first time I have had an opportunity in the six years I have served in the House to speak on the significance of Louis Riel and the contribution he has made to the Province of Manitoba, the development of western Canada and the development of Canada as a whole.
I have introduced resolutions under the old Standing Order 43, calling for the pardon of Louis Riel when that was being sought by the Metis people themselves. Their position with regard to a pardon has changed and they no longer believe that a pardon would be sufficient to recognize the role Louis David Riel has played.
I have lived all of my life in Manitoba. I was always amazed that we did not study Louis Riel very much in school. We learned about the railway and that he was a person from Saskatchewan causing trouble with the railway. We talked about how Manitoba was developed as a province but the actual study of the contribution made by Louis Riel and the Metis was passed over in one or two days.
As a former teacher of history I will certainly not blame the teachers or those who wrote the curriculum. It is a matter of their perception of history at that time. They had their vision of Canada as a nation of the English and the French. They had their vision of Canada in the west developing as a natural consequence of the expansion of the Anglo-Saxon and French population base from the east to the west in this country. That was a natural oversight and I do not think it can be said that it
February 24, 1986

Metis Nation
was a matter of racial prejudice or tension that existed between the English and the French in Manitoba.
We now have a chance to move forward. I have gone to many of the communities in my riding where the Metis live and I have noted that there is more study being done of the role of Louis Riel and of the significant contributions the Metis people have made to Manitoba. In many ways, the fall-out of the French language dispute which occurred in Manitoba just two years ago has helped to remind people of the original contribution of Louis Riel and the fact that he, through his emissaries, negotiated with the Government of John A. Macdonald and has guaranteed the rights of the English and the French in that province. That is something which many politicians refuse to recognize even at this time. But there was a constitutional clause which guaranteed the rights of English and French groups and certain religions and also recognized that there was a group of people, the Metis of Maniotoba, who had the right to their own land. That is something which is still sought by the Metis people. They have hired Thomas Berger, a former Justice of the British Columbia Supreme Court, to represent them on this issue through the courts. That is one route the Metis people of Manitoba have taken to try to resolve the land issue.
Other things are happening as well within my province and 1 would like to talk about them. One of the previous speakers who now represents the Province of British Columbia, was born and brought up in the Province of Manitoba. Fie mentioned that there are other problems the Metis people face. The Metis people are really a nation which was founded in Canada as a result of the history of our country. There was the intermixing of the native population with those who came to Canada because of the fur trade and the Hudson's Bay Company, and for homesteading. The Metis people, especially in the riding I represent, but in other parts of Manitoba and western Canada as well, have not had the type of economic development or Government assistance from which other Canadians have benefited. We have all heard the statistics given by Hon. Members, including myself, in the House. We have talked about the need for native people to get postsecondary education, to become doctors, lawyers, nurses, social workers and to develop their own businesses. We have also talked about the terrible statistics with respect to the health of the Metis and other aboriginal people. We know about the tuberculosis, alcoholism and other diseases from which many native people suffer. We have heard of their mortality, their shorter life-span. It is no wonder that that has become a real concern because as I travelled around western Canada 1 saw the type of housing of the Metis people. I know of the lack of water and sewage. Quite often their drinking water is completely unsafe. They have no protection as do the Treaty Indians. The federal Government has recognized responsibility to provide education and water and sewage for Treaty Indians. Mind you, that is a responsibility which federal Governments have reneged on for many years and it is still an issue in many of the regions in my riding. In fact, the federal Government
has not provided adequate water and sewage and is making no real attempt to come up with a system to provide them. We can compare what is happening with the Treaty Indians, who at least have the protection of the treaties. The federal Government is supposed to provide some basic necessities for the Treaty Indians. In many cases, they are much better off than the Metis people who are basically without any protection, without any land or real home site in western Canada. Some of them have land in the southern parts of the provinces, but in the north the Metis people were shoved off the reserves and tended to live in communities that were adjacent to reserves but without any clear title to the very land that they, their fathers, and sometimes their grandfathers and grandmothers-not to be sexist-had lived on for years. They trapped that land and fished off its shores. They had existed there. They were brought up there and their families were raised there. They were brought up there and their families were raised there. But there was no legal recognition of that fact. They were excluded from homestead Acts, for example.
1 am proud to say that within Manitoba much of that has changed. There has been a recognition that there needs to be an improvement in the way of life of native people whether they are Treaty Indians and officially under the sponsorship of the federal Government or whether they are Metis people who in many cases have to rely on provincial Governments for their support.
It is interesting that the Metis National Council, in its issue which came out this winter-and which includes a copy of the draft resolution submitted by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior-talks about how the Council sat down with Premier Pawley and how they agreed on the need to promote Metis economic development. They talked about the increased need to recognize Metis culture and heritage, about the need for Metis participation in the delivery of services and programs to meet their own particular needs and circumstances, and they agreed that the Metis people must participate in Government decision-making in matters which directly affect them. So there is a process which has been going on in northern Manitoba, where the bulk of the Metis live, although they live elsewhere as well, to ensure that we do what we can to aid in the development of the native people, to make sure they have education and levels of services in their communities commensurate with their size. That is happening but it is still only a partial effort. There are things the federal and provincial Governments must do in order to ensure that native people, whether they be Treaty Indians or Metis, have that which they need in order to develop.
As a New Democrat from Manitoba, I think we have made great strides in the last 20 years in my province. I am sure that other Hon. Members from Manitoba, regardless to which Party they belong, would agree that this has happened. But that is not to say that all has happened that should have happened or that all is perfect for the native people in the province.
In the last 10 or 15 years, housing programs sponsored by both the federal and provincial Governments have increased

February 24, 1986
the quality of housing. When I first moved north in 1970 there were Metis people living in tar-paper shacks in Manitoba. I know from my travels to other parts of Canada that the same thing could be said of Ontario and other parts of this country as well. There were almost no native teachers in northern Manitoba. There were no native social workers. There was no one with native ancestry taking training to become an engineer. There were very few native people in any university program whatsoever. The idea of a native businessman was something that no one would have thought would ever exist unless it was to do with some freighting for the Hudson's Bay Company. That was their status some 20 short years ago in the Province of Manitoba. We now have a program, again sponsored by both federal and provincial money-actually a number of programs-which encourage natives to become teachers. Over 300 people have completed those programs and are now teaching within Manitoba. There is a program for the development of native social workers. There is a program for nursing. There are also other programs to encourage the economic development of native people both individually and through their communities.
The history of Louis Riel does not have to be debated in this House. I think all of us recognize his contribution. There may be some who would argue about the details of it. However, there can be no legitimate debate with respect to the fact that Louis Riel was the founder of Manitoba and that through the process he established the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were able to develop in a way which may not have happened had the negotiations not taken place between the people of the Red River settlement and the Government of Manitoba in the years 1869-70. That was a negotiation which took place between the people who lived in Red River and the people who were running the Government in Canada. It set out the Manitoba Act, which is the basic constitution of the province. It obviously influenced the development of our province. By anyone's definition that would be good enough to ensure that Louis Riel be recognized as the founder of Manitoba and a legitimate Father of Confederation in his own right. I hope that would not be questioned by anyone in this House.
What we have to do is to find the best means to further the economic development of the people of Metis ancestry, just as we have to ensure that we develop the possibility for economic development for the other aboriginal people of Canada. We will make mistakes as we go along that road. However, it is incumbent upon us to recognize that, when Government talks about restraint, hopefully, in the Budget which is to be tabled two days' hence, we will not find that programs which would enhance native economic development are being cut.
Even though we will make mistakes with regard to the development of economic opportunities for native people and even though we offer training programs, such as the one with regard to limestone development in northern Manitoba-a massive development under the native affirmative action program-we must ensure that certain people in our society do not try to turn us from the road we must follow. Even though
Metis Nation
from time to time we may find that native leaders and native businessmen will make mistakes, perhaps with money which comes from the Province of Manitoba or the coffers of the federal Government, we should not allow certain elements of our society to turn us from the road we must follow. It will take a massive commitment not only to solve the health problems and to provide basic housing but to provide the proper education, training and economic development opportunities for these people. Anyone who says otherwise is not really thinking.
As I said earlier, there will be failures as we go along this road. However, we as representatives of the people of Canada should be willing to accept that. We should be willing to get up and say that there will be problems, but that should be no reason to cut off funding. Certainly, there were problems with some native leaders who perhaps misused money. In some cases it was done illegally and in others it was done in ways not very different from the way federal Cabinets sometimes deal with money. That is to say money was spent in ways which we would not judge to be the wisest expenditures of money.
However, when we hear such voices-and they are often from the right, but sometimes they come from other parts of the political spectrum as well-we should say that, yes, there will be failure and that, yes, there has been abuse, but let us look at what we should be doing together in the country to help those who need our help the most. That should be the criteria of the programs. We should be judging the programs on the basis of what we can do to help. We should ask how this can best be achieved. We should say no to those people who are benefiting or trying to benefit by attacking the native people and yes to those who seek to help them.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGAR-BEET INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) ONTARIO AND QUEBEC CORN PRODUCERS
AGRICULTURE-SUGAR-BEET INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) ONTARIO AND QUEBEC CORN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 4 I rose in the House to inquiry as to the Government's policy regarding sugar. I did this because the sugar industry is in trouble. Last year, for the first time in 60 years, no sugar-beets were planted in Alberta. Two weeks ago, the refinery in Winnipeg closed, putting 95 people out of a job and possibly spelling the beginning of the end for the sugar industry in Manitoba. In Ontario and Quebec, several hundred sugar-beet growers, along with the 25,000 farmers who grow corn for the high fructose corn syrup market, face an uncertain future.

The normal and artificial evolution of raw sugar prices on the world market over the last four years is just about to put out of business the Canadian sugar beet industry.

Ninety-five per cent of world trade in sugar consists of long-term buying and selling agreements. The remaining 5 per cent is sold on the free market, which is generally conceded to be a dumping ground for excess sugar. In most of the years since 1960, world production has exceeded consumption and as a result, the prices in this small free market have been greatly depressed, often to but a fraction of the real cost of production for any country. Canada buys about 90 per cent of its sugar on this free market at bargain prices. However, unlike other sugar-producing developed countries, Canada forces its own producers to meet and compete against these artificially low prices.
Our sugar industry is obviously being damaged by these imports, but the Government refuses to refer the matter to the Canadian Import Tribunal. Unlike the Government of the United States, it refuses to support producers by instituting a floor price for raw sugar. In short, regarding sugar policy, this Government is continuing the non-policy of the last Government.

February 24, 1986
It has been argued that for health reasons, we should not encourage an increase in consumption of sugar. However, that does not mean that we should let Canadian sugar-beet and corn growers go out of business. Do not forget that over 90 per cent of our sugar comes from overseas but we go on consuming sugar. The question really is: Where should it be grown?
It has already been argued that it is just good business practice to keep importing sugar at artificially low prices as long as we can. For some people that might be good, but is it good for Canada as a whole? I say hardly.
Never mind that cheap sugar is dumped on the market at below the cost of production. Never mind that this makes it even more difficult for developing nations to diversify their agricultural production into food crops for local consumption. Never mind that it further threatens our way of life by throwing farmers, machinery manufacturers and refinery workers out of work and onto the unemployment rolls. Never mind that the U.S., the European Community, Japan and other developed sugar-producing countries protect their producers.
The hard fact is that consumers in this country tend not to benefit from the low-price policy. If we were benefiting from that policy, why have we not noticed a decrease in the price of ice cream, candy, soft drinks, beer, bread, sweetened yogurt or frozen and canned foods? It sounds like the same old story that we have been hearing recently in the House about the petroleum indistry and the long wait for the lowering of the prices of gasoline.
The decline in the domestic sugar industry also means that consumers are subjected to wild fluctuations in the price of sugar. Most people in the industry remember the tripling in price that occurred in 1980 when foreign supplies ran low. Prices in Canada jumped three times. If that is what the Government means by good business practice, it sounds a lot like short-term pain for long-term pain. As the President of the UPA recently stated:

"We believe that it would not be in the national interest to let such a strategic industry disappear."

The Minister himself was getting to the crux of the matter last October when he stated that we in this country ought to think pretty long and hard about being totally dependent on somebody else for an essential food.
But the Minister has had enough time to think. He has been putting off the decision for too long. It will be March next week. Last week, or rather last year I asked why this delay.
Last April, he replied:
We wish the decision could have been made earlier but we are preparing a long-term policy and it takes time.
Adjournment Debate
He went on to say:
1 repeat, a decision must be announced this week because sugar-beet growers will have to plant their crop very soon. If they do not plant this year we will lose a major agricultural industry.
In January the Minister told us that a national sugar-beet policy would be unveiled by February 10-

In his words "at the very latest". Why was the announcement not made? Given the importance of the industry, why has there been such a delay? Is the Government siding with some factions of the industry which benefit greatly from cheap sugar at the producers' expense? Is the Government afraid to establish a national sugar policy because it has just killed the National Energy Program? Is the Government afraid of following the example of other countries in erecting barriers against artificially low-priced sugar? Is the Canadian sugar industry an indirect early casualty to free trade negotiations?
If the Minister fails again this week to make a clear statement on the issue, the Government will reinforce the impression that the sugar industry in Canada is expendable. Producers in other sectors, producers of eggs, hatching eggs, chickens, dairy products, hogs, fruits and vegetables will grimly take note. They and other Canadians will be filled with foreboding as they see their Government by its inactions submitting its citizens to a buffeting by factors beyond their control.
The Government had to decide whether it wants a sugar industry as part of Canada's agricultural economy. The Government has to decide soon, Mr. Speaker.

industrial users were there. Everybody was there except for the Province of Manitoba representatives. 1 found that unfortunate and I think the Hon. Member should know that.
