subtopic: THE ECONOMY-INTEREST RATE LEVELS. (B) EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR. (C) GOVERNMENT POLICY
THE ECONOMY-INTEREST RATE LEVELS. (B) EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR. (C) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 3 the Canadian dollar fell below the 70-cent mark for the first time in history. Three days later the Bank of Canada borrowed $2.4 billion to add to our foreign exchange reserves, which are used to defend the value of the dollar, and began intervening heavily in the market to prop up our currency. The Bank of Canada then jacked up interest rates by more than two-thirds of a percentage point in a further effort to attract
investors. Prime interest rates rose within hours from 11.5 per cent to 12.25 per cent, their highest rate in 15 months.
The Government takes the position that this action to boost the dollar was necessary in order to halt a speculative attack on our currency which, according to the Government, was prompted by "negative sentiment" about our economy. Clearly there is doubt and uncertainty, but it is due less to inherent problems with the economy than to the Government's lack of resolve or agenda to deal with those problems. The Government's costly intervention in the market did nothing to address this fundamental problem which was what triggered speculation in the first place.
The decline of the value of the dollar over the last few months is due to a lack of confidence internationally in the ability of the Conservative Government to manage the economy. Even before the dollar fell below the 70-cent mark, the Government was devoting considerable effort to attempts to keep its value up. It was obvious because short-term interest rates have been steadily increasing over the last few months. The higher interest rate policy did not stop the dollar from sinking to an historic low. When we consider our domestic economy, the consequences of continually raising interest rates give much cause for concern.
Higher interest rates discourage spending and encourage saving. This is not a good prescription when our goal is to sustain and strengthen economic recovery. Higher interest rates mean it costs more to borrow. Therefore, businesses cannot afford to expand or to hire new staff, consumers have to reconsider or postpone large purchases, and people renegotiating mortgages will pay more. Higher interest rates mean less economic growth and a larger deficit, because higher interest rates mean more interest added to payments on the national debt.
The recession of 1981-82 was the worst since the Depression. We are recovering from it now, and our first objective should be to do all we can to build on that recovery. We should be concentrating on jobs, economic growth, and stability. Rising interest rates constitute a major obstacle to achieving those goals. Unless interest rates drop, economic growth will slacken and we will have no further improvement in the employment rate.
The Government sees deficit reduction as the key to lower interest rates on the assumption that a reduced deficit will revive international confidence. The other side of that coin is that Government restraint measures aimed at cutting the deficit take money out of the domestic economy, thereby making economic growth and job creation harder to come by.
The Government must act promptly to ease interest rates in order to avoid undercutting economic growth. It must make a serious effort to address the matter of declining international confidence in the ability of the Conservative Government to manage the economy. We cannot afford any more flashy but shortsighted manoeuvrings on international currency markets. We cannot afford any more bank bail-outs or tax concessions to

February 24, 1986
large corporations, or open-ended tax exemptions. Nor can we afford to let high interest rates choke off economic recovery, or tax away the purchasing power of low and middle-income Canadians. This week the Government will bring down its second Budget as well as the Estimates for its expenditures over the next year. Let us hope that the Government moves to correct the inequities arising from its first Budget and to articulate, through new proposals, its view of the way to revitalize the economy and strengthen recovery.

CRIMINAL CODE-ACQUISITION OF FIREARMS BY PERSONS CONVICTED ON GUN CHARGES

that they would be discussing the whole issue of tougher gun control regulations. 1 am sure that when he got together with his counterparts, the provincial Attorneys General and Ministers of Justice, they undoubtedly discussed the usual concerns that are raised whenever tougher firearm regulations are dis-sussed. There are a good many of those concerns, as Members know.
There are concerns raised by hunters who feel that it is their right, their privilege, and that it dates back historically, to bear arms and to use those arms. There are the concerns that are usually expressed by target shooters, and I have them in my own constituency, who feel they have the right, and they have had it for many years, to acquire and possess weapons and use them for target practice. Many of them belong to target clubs and use them within an organized club setting. There are the concerns, of course, of those people who have antique guns. In fact, this past Christmas season I visited a home which had a wall full of antique guns. It is a long-standing historical right to collect guns and to have them around. There are also the concerns of those who use guns in their profession or occupation. That is another long-standing right. All of these various concerns, whether it be hunters, target shooters, gun collectors or professionals who use these guns in their occupation, have certain rights that have been built up over time. They have some legitimate concerns and reasons for having possession and being allowed to have possession of firearms.
Having said all of that, I think it is quite clear that the public also has a right to be protected in their homes and on the streets from the fear that somebody may have a gun and use it to injure or kill them or their families. I believe that right overrides the rights of the hunters, target shooters, gun collectors and professionals. It is a right that we must look after and protect. This must be done through a form of
tougher gun control. One way to accomplish this is to take the recommendation of that coroner's jury in Metropolitan Toronto and amend the Criminal Code accordingly. That would go a small way toward giving us some further protection.
The Parliamentary Secretary has had the benefit of consulting with the Minister and the Minister has had the benefit of consulting with his colleagues. I hope that tonight the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to tell us that there will be changes, that there will be tougher gun controls, what they will be and when they will be introduced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-ACQUISITION OF FIREARMS BY PERSONS CONVICTED ON GUN CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his question. I would like to be able to tell him tonight that the details of the amendments he is seeking to the Criminal Code will be in the next Bill. I can tell him that his concerns are shared by the Department.
I am assured by the Minister that when the next set of amendments are brought to the Criminal Code, these gun control provisions will be the subject matter of amendments. This decision of the Minister flows from his meeting with the Attorneys General of the provinces that was held last week.
When these amendments are brought forward, we can have a debate in the House that will enable all Members to discuss these rights to which the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has referred. Surely, people have a right to be protected but there are also the rights of gun collectors and hunters. I believe that we can achieve a just balance and it is with this in mind that I think these amendments will be brought forward soon.
